Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let $H$ be a predictable
process on $[0,T]$, where $T\ge0$, with $E\int_0^TH_s^2ds<\infty$. Extend $H$ by zero after $T$ when applying the global continuous-version theorem, and let
$M_t=\int_0^tH_s\,dB_s$ be the continuous version of
[[thm-ito-integral-process-has-a-continuous-martingale-version]]. Then
$$E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|M_t|^2\le4\,E\int_0^TH_s^2\,ds .$$
The left-hand side is finite and does not depend on the chosen version, since
any two continuous versions are indistinguishable. Every continuous version of
the integral process satisfies the same bound. The path supremum in this
expectation means its measurable version $S_D=\sup_{q\in D}|M_q|$ on the
countable scaled dyadic grid $D$ (including both endpoints). Continuity
identifies it with the path supremum on a measurable event of probability one.
Indistinguishability here uses that full-event convention, as in the cited
continuous-version theorem, without assuming completeness of the filtration.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let $H$ be a locally
square-integrable predictable process
[[def-locally-square-integrable-predictable-brownian-integrand]] with localized
integral $H\cdot B$ in the progressively measurable version of
[[thm-localized-ito-integral]], with its measurable-full-event convention
for indistinguishability. The filtration satisfies the usual conditions and
local energy is finite almost surely on every finite horizon, as required by
the local-integrability definition. Let $\tau$ be a
stopping time [[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]]. Then the process
$s\mapsto(H\cdot B)_{s\wedge\tau}$ and the localized integral of the process
$1_{[0,\tau]}H$ are indistinguishable:
$$(H\cdot B)_{t\wedge\tau}=\int_0^t1_{[0,\tau]}(s)H_s\,dB_s\qquad\text{for every }t\ge0\text{, up to indistinguishability}.$$
In particular, for $H$ of finite energy this reduces to the stopping identity
of [[thm-localized-ito-integral]], and for $\tau\equiv\infty$ it is the
definition of the localized integral.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and let $d\ge1$ be a finite integer. An
$\mathbb R^d$-valued process $B=(B_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **standard
$d$-dimensional Brownian motion** if:

1. $B_0=0$ almost surely;
2. for every finite list $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_n$, the vector increments
   $$B_{t_j}-B_{t_{j-1}},\qquad 1\le j\le n,$$
   are mutually independent and have laws
   $N_d(0,(t_j-t_{j-1})I_d)$; and
3. there is one measurable event $A$ with $P(A)=1$ such that
   $t\mapsto B_t(\omega)$ is continuous from $[0,\infty)$ to
   $\mathbb R^d$ for every $\omega\in A$.

Equivalently, its $d$ coordinate processes $B^\alpha=(B_t^\alpha)_{t\ge0}$
are independent standard one-dimensional Brownian motions. Here independence
of the processes means the following precise assertion. Put
$I=[0,\infty)$ and equip $\mathbb R^I$ with its cylinder sigma-algebra. The
maps
$$ \Phi_\alpha:\Omega\longrightarrow\mathbb R^I, \qquad \Phi_\alpha(\omega)(t)=B_t^\alpha(\omega), \qquad 1\le\alpha\le d, $$
are independent random elements.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Let
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space with a continuous-time
filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. All processes here
are real-valued and indexed by $[0,\infty)$. AC is inherited from the cited
continuous-time-filtration interface, whose separate martingale clause uses
conditional expectation. Once the filtered probability space and stopping
times are given, the progressive and predictable constructions below make no
additional choice: they use only generated sigma-algebras and product
rectangles.

1. **Progressively measurable.** A process $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **progressively measurable** relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when for every
   $t\ge0$ the restricted map
   $[0,t]\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$, $(s,\omega)\mapsto X_s(\omega)$, is
   measurable for the product sigma-algebra
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$
   [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]].

2. **Time-zero and interval generators.** On the product space
   $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$, let $\mathcal P$ be the sigma-algebra generated by
   the family
   $$\mathcal G:=\bigl\{(s,u]\times A:\ 0\le s<u<\infty,\ A\in\mathcal F_s\bigr\}\ \cup\ \bigl\{\{0\}\times A:\ A\in\mathcal F_0\bigr\}.$$
   The interval generators with $s=0$ are included, so $(0,u]\times A$ with
   $A\in\mathcal F_0$ is a generator. The sigma-algebra $\mathcal P$ exists by
   [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]] and is called the
   **predictable sigma-algebra**. A process $H=(H_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **predictable** when the map $(s,\omega)\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is
   $\mathcal P$-measurable. For a finite horizon $T>0$ we write
   $\mathcal P_T$ for the sigma-algebra on $[0,T]\times\Omega$ generated by the
   same family restricted to $u\le T$ together with the time-zero generators;
   this is the trace of $\mathcal P$ on $[0,T]\times\Omega$. Indeed, the
   trace of an interval generator is empty when $s\ge T$, and otherwise is
   $(s,\min(u,T)]\times A$, while time-zero generators are unchanged.
   Conversely every listed finite-horizon generator is such a trace.

3. **Sections, adaptedness, and null sets.** Two structural conventions are
   used repeatedly and are part of the definition.
   (a) Every generator is a measurable rectangle of
   $\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$, hence
   $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$; the time-zero
   generator $\{0\}\times A$ has $dt\otimes P$-measure zero for every $A$. A
   set in $\mathcal P$ has its section at each fixed time $s$ in $\mathcal F_s$:
   sets with that section property form a sigma-algebra, and each generator
   has the property by the increasing-filtration condition. Its section at
   each fixed $\omega$ is Borel in time, by the same sigma-algebra argument.
   (b) If a process is predictable then it is progressively measurable: for
   $s\le t$ the section $\omega\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is $\mathcal F_s$-measurable
   $\subseteq\mathcal F_t$-measurable, and the progressive-measurability claim
   is the restriction of the joint map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$; the restriction
   of a $\mathcal P$-measurable map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$ is measurable for
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$ because every generator with $u\le t$
   lies in that product sigma-algebra and the generators with $u>t$ have
   intersection with $[0,t]\times\Omega$ of the form $(s,t]\times A$ with
   $s<t$ and $A\in\mathcal F_s$, or the empty set when $s\ge t$.
   The time-zero generators also lie in
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$.

The family $\mathcal G$ need not itself contain the whole space, but a finite intersection
of generators is empty or again a generator, or a time-zero generator, because
$(s,u]\cap(s',u']=(s\vee s',u\wedge u']$ and $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_{s\vee s'}$
whenever $A\in\mathcal F_s$, $A'\in\mathcal F_{s'}$, while
$\{0\}\times A$ is disjoint from every interval generator, including
$(0,u]\times A'$. Two time-zero generators intersect in
$\{0\}\times(A\cap A')$ with $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_0$.
Thus the family consisting of the whole space
together with finite intersections of generators is a pi-system generating
$\mathcal P$; this is the structural fact used by the density theorem below.

Because predictability is a measurability requirement for the joint map, it is
preserved by pointwise limits, products and linear combinations of predictable
processes. A deterministic function $h$ of time defines a predictable process
exactly when $h$ is Borel measurable: the sets $C$ for which
$C\times\Omega\in\mathcal P$ form a sigma-algebra containing the intervals
$(s,u]$ and $\{0\}$, hence all Borel sets. Conversely, take any fixed
$\omega\in\Omega$ (a probability space is nonempty) and use the Borel
time-section property from 3(a) on every inverse image of an open set.
This single choice uses no choice axiom. In particular the
indicators $1_{[0,u]}$ and $1_{(0,u]}$ are predictable for every deterministic
$u\ge0$, and the process $s\mapsto 1_{s\le\tau(\omega)}$ for a stopping time
$\tau$ [[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]] is predictable, since
$$\{(s,\omega):s>\tau(\omega)\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}(q,\infty)\times\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}\bigcup_{n>q}(q,n]\times\{\tau<q\}$$
is a countable union of generators: for rational $q>0$ one has
$\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q'<q,\ q'\in\mathbb Q}\{\tau\le q'\}\in\mathcal F_q$. The
complement of that set inside $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$ is the event of the
indicator, so $1_{[0,\tau]}$ is predictable; its left-continuity in the time
variable is the visual form of the same computation.

No completeness of the filtration and no right continuity of $(\mathcal F_t)$
is used or assumed. Apart from the inherited ambient assumption just recorded,
the constructions in this definition are choice-free.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space and let
$(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$ be a continuous-time filtration
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]].

1. A map $\tau:\Omega\to[0,\infty]$ (infinite values allowed) is a **stopping
   time** for $(\mathcal F_t)$ when
   $$\{\tau\le t\}\in\mathcal F_t\qquad\text{for every }t\ge0 .$$
2. For a stopping time $\tau$ its **stopped sigma-algebra** is
   $$\mathcal F_\tau:=\{A\in\mathcal F:A\cap\{\tau\le t\}\in\mathcal F_t \text{ for every }t\ge0\}.$$

The following facts are used below, and each is a direct set computation.

(a) $\mathcal F_\tau$ is a sigma-algebra: $\emptyset\cap\{\tau\le
    t\}=\emptyset\in\mathcal F_t$; for $A\in\mathcal F_\tau$ one has
    $A^c\cap\{\tau\le t\}=\{\tau\le t\}\setminus(A\cap\{\tau\le t\})\in\mathcal
    F_t$; and for a sequence $A_n\in\mathcal F_\tau$ the union satisfies
    $\bigl(\bigcup_nA_n\bigr)\cap\{\tau\le t\}=\bigcup_n(A_n\cap\{\tau\le
    t\})\in\mathcal F_t$. All operations are literal, not modulo null sets, and
    no completeness of the filtration is assumed.
(b) If $\tau\equiv t_0<\infty$ is deterministic, then
    $A\cap\{\tau\le t\}$ is $A$ for $t\ge t_0$ and $\emptyset$ for $t<t_0$, so
    $\mathcal F_\tau=\bigcap_{t\ge t_0}\mathcal F_t=\mathcal F_{t_0}$, where
    the last equality follows because the intersection includes its least
    member $\mathcal F_{t_0}$. If $\tau\equiv\infty$, then every test event
    $\{\tau\le t\}$ is empty and $\mathcal F_\tau=\mathcal F$.
(c) Suppose the filtration is right-continuous. Then $\tau$ is a stopping time
    if and only if $\{\tau<t\}\in\mathcal F_t$ for every $t>0$. Indeed
    $$\{\tau<t\}=\bigcup_{n\ge1}\{\tau\le t-\tfrac1n\}$$
    (with the terms for $t-\tfrac1n<0$ read as the empty set, since
    $\tau\ge0$), which gives the forward implication; conversely
    $$\{\tau\le t\}=\bigcap_{n\ge1}\{\tau<t+\tfrac1n\},$$
    and $\bigcap_n\mathcal F_{t+1/n}=\bigcap_{s>t}\mathcal F_s=\mathcal F_t$ by
    right-continuity together with monotonicity of the filtration.
(d) Under the same right-continuity assumption, for $A\in\mathcal F$ one has
    $A\in\mathcal F_\tau$ if and only if $A\cap\{\tau<t\}\in\mathcal F_t$ for
    every $t>0$: the forward implication follows from
    $A\cap\{\tau<t\}=\bigcup_n(A\cap\{\tau\le t-\tfrac1n\})$ and the converse
    from $A\cap\{\tau\le t\}=\bigcap_n(A\cap\{\tau<t+\tfrac1n\})$ together with
    $\bigcap_n\mathcal F_{t+1/n}=\mathcal F_t$.

Because the two versions of each test are interchangeable exactly when the
filtration is right-continuous, the convention is recorded here once: the
Brownian strong Markov theorem is stated for the usual augmentation, which is
right-continuous, and the raw-filtration statements use the non-strict test
directly. No choice principle is used by this definition.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Fix $T>0$. For predictable
$H,K$ with finite energy $E\int_0^TH^2ds,E\int_0^TK^2ds<\infty$ the integrals
$\int_0^TH\,dB$ of
[[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]] satisfy
$$\int_0^T(H+K)\,dB=\int_0^TH\,dB+\int_0^TK\,dB,\qquad \int_0^T(aH)\,dB=a\int_0^TH\,dB\quad(a\in\mathbb R),$$
and the identities are equalities of $L^2(P)$-classes (almost sure
equalities). Moreover the map $H\mapsto\int_0^TH\,dB$ is an isometry,
$$E\Bigl(\int_0^TH\,dB\Bigr)^2=E\int_0^TH^2ds=\|H\|^2_{L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)},$$
it takes values in the mean-zero subspace of $L^2(P)$, and the bilinear cross
identity
$$E\Bigl[\Bigl(\int_0^TH\,dB\Bigr)\Bigl(\int_0^TK\,dB\Bigr)\Bigr]=E\int_0^TH_sK_s\,ds$$
holds for all such $H,K$. In particular the image of the map is a closed
subspace of $L^2(P)$ isometric to the predictable $L^2$ space of $H$'s, and
$H\mapsto\int_0^TH\,dB$ is injective up to the $(\mathrm dt\otimes P)$-class.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and work under the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]: a filtered probability space
with a standard Brownian motion $B$ adapted to the filtration, with increments
$B_t-B_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ of law $N(0,t-s)$. Fix $T>0$ and an
elementary predictable integrand
$$H_s=\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\xi_k\,1_{(t_k,t_{k+1}]}(s),\qquad 0=t_0<\cdots<t_m=T,$$
with bounded $\mathcal F_{t_k}$-measurable coefficients $\xi_k$. The **Ito
integral of $H$ against $B$** is the process
$$I_t(H):=\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\xi_k\bigl(B_{t\wedge t_{k+1}}-B_{t\wedge t_k}\bigr),\qquad 0\le t\le T,$$
also written $\int_0^tH_s\,dB_s$ or $(H\cdot B)_t$. The sum is finite and is
evaluated with the Brownian path of the given representative; on the event
where $t\mapsto B_t$ is continuous it is continuous in $t$, and $I_0(H)=0$
because $0\wedge t_k=0$ for every $k$.

Three conventions are part of the definition.

1. **Adaptedness and continuity.** For fixed $t$, each summand
   $\xi_k(B_{t\wedge t_{k+1}}-B_{t\wedge t_k})$ is $\mathcal F_t$-measurable:
   if $t<t_k$, the Brownian difference and hence the summand are zero; if
   $t\ge t_k$, then $\mathcal F_{t_k}\subseteq\mathcal F_t$, while
   $B_{t\wedge u}$ is $\mathcal F_t$-measurable for every $u$ because
   $t\wedge u\le t$. Thus
   $I(H)$ is adapted. For each fixed $\omega$ the map
   $t\mapsto B_{t\wedge t_{k+1}}(\omega)-B_{t\wedge t_k}(\omega)$ is continuous
   outside the single exceptional null set of (H) on which the Brownian path is
   discontinuous; the finite sum is therefore continuous on the same event.

2. **Linearity on a common refinement.** If $H$ and $K$ are elementary
   integrands and a partition refines both representations, then the defining
   sums of $H$, $K$, $H+K$ and $aH$ are taken over that common partition, and
   the finite sums give $I_t(H+K)=I_t(H)+I_t(K)$ and $I_t(aH)=aI_t(H)$ for real
   $a$ identically. In particular $I_t(H)-I_t(K)=I_t(H-K)$ for the
   elementary integrand $H-K$ represented on that refinement. This is a
   rearrangement of finitely many terms, not a limiting statement.

3. **Dependence on the representation is temporary.** The definition attaches
   $I_t(H)$ to a *chosen* elementary representation.
   [[lem-elementary-ito-integral-is-independent-of-the-step-representation]] proves that
   two representations that agree $(\mathrm dt\otimes P)$-almost everywhere
   produce the same random variables almost surely at each fixed time, so that
   $I_t(H)$ is a function of the $(\mathrm dt\otimes P)$-class of $H$ alone.
   Until then, every statement about an elementary integrand names the
   representation it uses.

The Axiom of Choice is declared because the standing hypothesis (H) is part of
the Brownian interface of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]], which assumes it; the
definition of the finite sum uses no choice. The countable-choice obligations
inherited from that interface are declared as dependencies of this item.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Fix $T>0$ and let
$\mathcal P_T$ be the predictable sigma-algebra on $[0,T]\times\Omega$
[[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]], with the finite
measure $\mathrm dt\otimes P$. Then the classes of bounded elementary
predictable integrands
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]] are dense in
$L^2([0,T]\times\Omega,\mathcal P_T,\mathrm dt\otimes P)$: for every
$\mathcal P_T$-measurable $H$ with $\int_0^T\!\!\int_\Omega H^2\,dP\,dt<\infty$
and every $\varepsilon>0$ there is a bounded elementary predictable integrand
$G$ with
$$\Bigl(\int_0^T\!\!\int_\Omega(H-G)^2\,dP\,dt\Bigr)^{1/2}<\varepsilon .$$
Equalities are equalities of $(\mathrm dt\otimes P)$-classes, so two elementary
integrands whose difference vanishes almost everywhere represent the same
approximant.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

The map $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[def-real-numbers]]) is an embedding of ordered
fields. Every real is approximated by rationals: for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and
rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with
$|x - \hat q| < \hat\varepsilon$. Consequently, strictly between any two
reals lies a rational.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: First take $m=1$. Put $Q_t=\int_0^tH_s^2ds$ and $M^*=\sup_{t\le T}|M_t|$. The continuous version makes $M^*$ measurable, and [F1] gives $\mathbb E(M^*)^2\le4\mathbb E Q_T<\infty$, so $\mathbb EM^*<\infty$.

Fix $\lambda>0$. Let $\tau$ be the first time $|M_t|\ge\lambda$, capped at $T$, and put $A_\lambda=\{M^*\ge\lambda\}$. Continuity and adaptation make $\tau$ a stopping time by [F9]–[F10], and $A_\lambda\in\mathcal F_\tau$: for each $t<T$, $A_\lambda\cap\{\tau\le t\}=\{\sup_{s\le t}|M_s|\ge\lambda\}$, whose supremum is measurable by [F10]; for $t\ge T$, the intersection is $A_\lambda\in\mathcal F_T\subseteq\mathcal F_t$ by the same terminal supremum fact. Let $R_t=Q_t-Q_{t\wedge\tau}$; this is continuous and adapted. Let $\sigma$ be its first hitting time of $\delta^2\lambda^2$, capped at $T$; it is a stopping time by [F9]–[F10], where $0<\delta<1/4$. The set $A_\lambda\cap\{\tau<s\}$ is the countable union, over rational $u>0$, of $(u,\infty)\times(A_\lambda\cap\{\tau\le u\})$. Each second factor belongs to $\mathcal F_u$ by $A_\lambda\in\mathcal F_\tau$. Thus it is predictable; intersecting with $\{s\le\sigma\}$ preserves predictability by [F4].

Define $N_t=\int_0^t1_{A_\lambda}1_{(\tau,\sigma]}(s)H_s\,dB_s.$ To identify its integral, round $\tau$ and $\sigma$ upward to a common dyadic grid, obtaining stopping times $\tau_n\le\sigma_n$ with $\tau_n\downarrow\tau$ and $\sigma_n\downarrow\sigma$. For an elementary predictable integrand on a refinement of this grid, the coefficient on $(t_k,t_{k+1}]$ after multiplying by $1_{A_\lambda}1_{(\tau_n,\sigma_n]}$ is measurable at $t_k$: the active event $\{\tau_n\le t_k<\sigma_n\}$ is in $\mathcal F_{t_k}$, and $A_\lambda\cap\{\tau_n\le t_k\}$ is in $\mathcal F_{t_k}$ because $A_\lambda\in\mathcal F_{\tau_n}$. Thus the finite-sum definition [F6] gives $\int_0^t1_{A_\lambda}1_{(\tau_n,\sigma_n]}H_s\,dB_s =1_{A_\lambda}\int_0^t1_{(\tau_n,\sigma_n]}H_s\,dB_s.$ For general predictable $H$, approximate in predictable $L^2$ by elementary integrands using [F7]; the isometry [F5] passes the identity to $H$ for this fixed grid. As $n\to\infty$, the interval indicators converge outside their two endpoint graphs, which are product-null; dominated convergence with majorant $H^2$ and [F5] pass the identity to $(\tau,\sigma]$. The stopping identity [F2] now identifies the right side with $1_{A_\lambda}(M_{t\wedge\sigma}-M_{t\wedge\tau})$. The accumulated energy of the integrand is at most $\delta^2\lambda^2 1_{A_\lambda}$ on every path. Thus [F1] gives $\mathbb E\sup_{t\le T}|N_t|^2 \le4\delta^2\lambda^2\mathbb P(A_\lambda).$ By [F2], on $A_\lambda$ this integral is the increment of $M$ after $\tau$ and before $\sigma$. On $\{M^*>2\lambda,\ Q_T^{1/2}\le\delta\lambda\}$ the threshold defining $\sigma$ is not reached before $T$, and after the first hit of $\lambda$ the continuous path moves by more than $\lambda$. Hence $\sup_{t\le T}|N_t|>\lambda$ on that event. Markov's inequality and the preceding display yield $\mathbb P(M^*>2\lambda,\ Q_T^{1/2}\le\delta\lambda) \le4\delta^2\mathbb P(M^*\ge\lambda).$

Split the event $\{M^*>2\lambda\}$ according to whether $Q_T^{1/2}>\delta\lambda$. The bound in step 2.1 gives $\mathbb P(M^*>2\lambda) \le\mathbb P(Q_T^{1/2}>\delta\lambda) +4\delta^2\mathbb P(M^*\ge\lambda).$ Integrating this inequality over $\lambda>0$ and applying Tonelli [F8] to $1_{\{(\lambda,\omega):\lambda<M^*(\omega)\}}$ and $1_{\{(\lambda,\omega):\lambda<Q_T(\omega)^{1/2}\}}$ gives $\mathbb EM^*\le\frac{2}{\delta}\mathbb E Q_T^{1/2} +8\delta^2\mathbb EM^*.$ With $\delta=1/4$, the last coefficient is $1/2$, so $\mathbb EM^*\le16\mathbb E Q_T^{1/2}$.

For general finite $m$, write $M=\sum_{j=1}^m M^j$ with $M_t^j=\int_0^tH_s^j\,dW_s^j$. Apply the scalar result of step 3.1 to each coordinate and then the finite-sum Cauchy–Schwarz inequality pathwise: $\mathbb E\sup_{t\le T}|M_t| \le16\sum_{j=1}^m\mathbb E\left(\int_0^T|H_s^j|^2ds\right)^{1/2} \le16\sqrt m\,\mathbb E\left(\int_0^T\sum_{j=1}^m|H_s^j|^2ds\right)^{1/2}.$ This is the claimed estimate. AC enters only through [A1] and the cited Brownian and Itô interfaces.

Assume AC. Fix finite integers $d,m\ge1$, $T>0$, and $N\ge1$ such that
$h=T/N\le1$. Work on a filtered probability space whose filtration is
right-continuous and contains every $P$-null subset of $\mathcal F$ in
$\mathcal F_0$. Let $W$ be an adapted standard
$m$-dimensional Brownian motion whose increments after time $s$ are
independent of $\mathcal F_s$. Let $X_0$ be finite, $\mathcal F_0$-measurable,
and independent of $\sigma(W_t-W_0:0\le t\le T)$.
Let $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ and
$g:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}$ be $C^1$. Assume finite constants
$\mu,c,D\ge0$ and an integer $q\ge1$ satisfy, for all $x,y\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$ \langle x-y,f(x)-f(y)\rangle\le\mu|x-y|^2,\qquad \|g(x)-g(y)\|_F^2\le c|x-y|^2, $$
$$ |f(x)-f(y)|^2\le D(1+|x|^q+|y|^q)|x-y|^2. $$
Here $|\cdot|$ is the Euclidean norm and $\|\cdot\|_F$ is the Frobenius
norm.

Set $t_k=kh$ and construct the grid approximation recursively by
$$ Y_0=X_0,\qquad Y_{k+1}=Y_k+f(Y_k)h+g(Y_k)(W_{t_{k+1}}-W_{t_k}),\quad 0\le k<N. $$
The output also includes the left-endpoint step process
$$ \bar Y_t=Y_k\quad(t_k\le t<t_{k+1}),\qquad \bar Y_T=Y_N, $$
and the continuous interpolation
$$ Y_t=Y_k+f(Y_k)(t-t_k)+g(Y_k)(W_t-W_{t_k})\quad(t_k\le t\le t_{k+1}). $$
The recursion makes the two interpolation formulas agree at every shared
endpoint. The finite recursion is defined pathwise: $C^1$ coefficients are
finite-valued, each $Y_k$ is finite almost surely by induction, and Brownian
paths are continuous. This algorithm defines no moment or convergence claim.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. If $0\le s,t$ and a real random variable
$X_t-X_s$ has law $N(0,|t-s|)$, then, for every integer $m\ge1$,
$$E|X_t-X_s|^{2m}=c_m|t-s|^m,$$
where
$$c_m=E|Z|^{2m}=(2m-1)!!=1\cdot3\cdots(2m-1)<\infty$$
for $Z\sim N(0,1)$. In particular, when $m\ge2$, this is the moment hypothesis
of the one-parameter Kolmogorov criterion with
$\alpha=2m$, $\beta=m-1$, and $C_T=c_m$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and let $d\ge1$ be a finite integer. An
$\mathbb R^d$-valued process $B=(B_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **standard
$d$-dimensional Brownian motion** if:

1. $B_0=0$ almost surely;
2. for every finite list $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_n$, the vector increments
   $$B_{t_j}-B_{t_{j-1}},\qquad 1\le j\le n,$$
   are mutually independent and have laws
   $N_d(0,(t_j-t_{j-1})I_d)$; and
3. there is one measurable event $A$ with $P(A)=1$ such that
   $t\mapsto B_t(\omega)$ is continuous from $[0,\infty)$ to
   $\mathbb R^d$ for every $\omega\in A$.

Equivalently, its $d$ coordinate processes $B^\alpha=(B_t^\alpha)_{t\ge0}$
are independent standard one-dimensional Brownian motions. Here independence
of the processes means the following precise assertion. Put
$I=[0,\infty)$ and equip $\mathbb R^I$ with its cylinder sigma-algebra. The
maps
$$ \Phi_\alpha:\Omega\longrightarrow\mathbb R^I, \qquad \Phi_\alpha(\omega)(t)=B_t^\alpha(\omega), \qquad 1\le\alpha\le d, $$
are independent random elements.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Fix $t\in[t_k,t_{k+1})$ and put $r_t=Y_t^h-\bar Y_t^h$ and $\delta=t-t_k$. By [F1], $r_t=\delta f(Y_k^h)+g(Y_k^h)(W_t-W_{t_k}).$ For even $r\ge2$, the finite-dimensional power inequality gives $|r_t|^r\le2^{r-1}\left(\delta^r|f(Y_k^h)|^r+ \|g(Y_k^h)\|_F^r|W_t-W_{t_k}|^r\right).$

Taking $y=0$ in the coefficient bounds gives $|f(x)|^2\le2|f(0)|^2+2D(1+|x|^q)|x|^2, \qquad \|g(x)\|_F^2\le2\|g(0)\|_F^2+2c|x|^2.$ Thus $|f(x)|^r\le C_r(1+|x|^{(q+2)r/2})$ and $\|g(x)\|_F^r\le C_r(1+|x|^r)$. The uniform all-moment premise therefore bounds both coefficient moments in step 1.1 uniformly over $h$ and $t$.

Each coordinate of $W_t-W_{t_k}$ has the Gaussian law in [F3], so [F2] and the finite-dimensional inequality $|z|^r\le C_{r,m}\sum_{j=1}^m|z_j|^r$ give $\mathbb E|W_t-W_{t_k}|^r\le C_{r,m}\delta^{r/2}$. Since $Y_k^h$ is $\mathcal F_{t_k}$-measurable and Brownian increments are independent of $\mathcal F_{t_k}$, conditioning in step 1.1 separates the coefficient factor from this Gaussian moment.

Using $0\le\delta\le h\le1$, so $\delta^r\le\delta^{r/2}$, steps 1.1, 2.1 and 2.2 yield $\mathbb E|Y_t^h-\bar Y_t^h|^r\le C_r h^{r/2}$ uniformly for $t<T$. At grid points the increment is zero by [F1], including $t=T$. The constants depend on $r,T,d,m,c,D,q,f(0),g(0)$ and the stated moment bounds, but not on $h$. AC is inherited only through [A1] and the declared Gaussian interfaces; no arbitrary-index choice is used in the estimate.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, let $d,m\ge1$ be finite, and fix $T>0$. Work on a
complete filtered probability space whose filtration is right-continuous and
contains every $P$-null subset of $\mathcal F$ in $\mathcal F_0$. Let $W$ be
an adapted standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion whose increments after
time $s$ are independent of $\mathcal F_s$. Let $X_0$ be finite and
$\mathcal F_0$-measurable, and independent of
$\sigma(W_t-W_0:0\le t\le T)$. Use the Euclidean state norm and Frobenius
matrix norm. Let $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ and
$g:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}$ be autonomous $C^1$ coefficients.
Assume finite constants $\mu,c,D\ge0$ and an integer $q\ge1$ satisfy, for
all $x,y\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$ \langle x-y,f(x)-f(y)\rangle\le\mu|x-y|^2,\qquad \|g(x)-g(y)\|_F^2\le c|x-y|^2, $$
$$ |f(x)-f(y)|^2\le D(1+|x|^q+|y|^q)|x-y|^2. $$
For each $0<h\le1$ with $N=T/h$ a positive integer, let $Y^h$ be the
continuous Euler–Maruyama interpolation and $\bar Y^h$ its left-endpoint step
process from [[alg-euler-maruyama-autonomous]], using this same $W$ and $X_0$.
Assume that for every finite $p\ge1$,
$$ \sup_{0<h\le1,\ T/h\in\mathbb N} \left(\mathbb E\sup_{t\le T}|Y_t^h|^p+ \mathbb E\sup_{t\le T}|\bar Y_t^h|^p\right)<\infty. $$
Then for every even integer $r\ge2$ there is a finite constant $C_r$, independent
of $h$, such that
$$ \sup_{0\le t\le T}\mathbb E|Y_t^h-\bar Y_t^h|^r\le C_r h^{r/2}. $$
The premise is an all-moment premise for this autonomous coefficient class; it
does not follow from the finite-$L^2$ moment bound alone.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let $m,d\ge1$ be finite
integers, let $B=(B^1,\dots,B^m)$ be a standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion,
and let $X$ be an $\mathbb R^d$-valued continuous Brownian Ito process
$$X^i_t=X^i_0+\int_0^tb^i_s\,ds+\sum_{k=1}^m\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s, \qquad i=1,\dots,d,$$
in the sense of [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]], including its usual-filtration and almost-sure coefficient-integrability conventions. Let
$f\in C^{1,2}([0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^d)$, meaning that $f,\partial_tf$,
$\partial_if$ and $\partial_i\partial_jf$ ($1\le i,j\le d$) exist and are
continuous. Then, up to indistinguishability, for every $t\ge0$
$$f(t,X_t)=f(0,X_0)+\int_0^t\Bigl(\partial_tf+\sum_ib^i\partial_if+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}\partial_i\partial_jf\Bigr)(s,X_s)\,ds+\sum_{i,k}\int_0^t\partial_if(s,X_s)\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s,$$
For the displayed integrands, intersect the measurable full events of continuity and the decomposition of $X$, and of coefficient integrability at all integer horizons. Its null complement belongs to $\mathcal F_0$ under the usual conditions. Set $X,X_0,b,\sigma$ to zero there. These representatives preserve all coefficient classes and the decomposition up to indistinguishability, with everywhere continuous $X$ and everywhere locally finite coefficient path integrals. All displayed integrands use these representatives.

The stochastic integrals are localized Ito integrals of the predictable
locally square-integrable integrands $\partial_if(\cdot,X)\sigma^{ik}$, and
$(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}_s=\sum_k\sigma^{ik}_s\sigma^{jk}_s$. In
differential form,
$df(t,X_t)=\bigl(\partial_tf+\sum_ib^i\partial_if+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}\partial_i\partial_jf\bigr)(t,X_t)\,dt+\sum_{i,k}\partial_if(t,X_t)\sigma^{ik}_t\,dB^k_t$.

Assume AC. Work on a complete filtered probability space
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{0\le t\le T},P)$ whose filtration is
right-continuous and contains every $P$-null subset of $\mathcal F$ in
$\mathcal F_0$. Let $m\ge1$ be finite, let
$W=(W^1,\dots,W^m)$ be an adapted standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion
[[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]] whose increments after time $s$ are
independent of $\mathcal F_s$, and let $H=(H^1,\dots,H^m)$ be a predictable
row-vector process [[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]] with
$\mathbb E\int_0^T\|H_s\|_2^2ds<\infty$. For
$$ M_t=\sum_{j=1}^m\int_0^tH_s^j\,dW_s^j, $$
the continuous version satisfies
$$ \mathbb E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|M_t| \le16\sqrt m\,\mathbb E\left(\int_0^T\|H_s\|_2^2ds\right)^{1/2}. $$

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

Let $t_0\le T$, let $u,a,b:[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $u,b\ge0$, and suppose

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t b(s)u(s)\,ds.$$

Then

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t a(s)b(s)\exp\!\left(\int_s^t b(r)\,dr\right)ds.$$

If $a$ is nondecreasing, this gives $u(t)\le a(t)\exp(\int_{t_0}^t b)$. The time-reflected form assumes $u(t)\le a(t)+\int_t^{t_0}b(s)u(s)\,ds$ for $t\le t_0$. In particular, when $a=A\ge0$ and $b=B\ge0$ are constant, the two orientations give $u(t)\le A e^{B|t-t_0|}$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]: $B$ is a standard Brownian
motion on a filtered probability space, adapted to $(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$,
with $B_t-B_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ of law $N(0,t-s)$ for $0\le s<t$.
For this localized-calculus definition the filtration satisfies the usual
conditions, as required by
[[def-locally-square-integrable-predictable-brownian-integrand]].

1. **Real continuous Brownian Ito process.** A real progressively measurable process
   $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **continuous Brownian Ito process** when there are
   * a finite real $\mathcal F_0$-measurable $X_0$,
   * a real progressively measurable process $b=(b_s)_{s\ge0}$
     [[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]] with
     $\int_0^t|b_s|\,ds<\infty$ almost surely for every finite $t\ge0$, and
   * a real predictable process $\sigma=(\sigma_s)_{s\ge0}$, locally
     square-integrable in the sense that $\int_0^t\sigma_s^2\,ds<\infty$
     almost surely for every finite $t$
     [[def-locally-square-integrable-predictable-brownian-integrand]],

   such that, up to equality at all times on a measurable probability-one event,
   $$X_t=X_0+\int_0^tb_s\,ds+\int_0^t\sigma_s\,dB_s,\qquad t\ge0,$$
   where the first integral is the pathwise Lebesgue integral of $s\mapsto
   b_s(\omega)$ and the second is the localized Ito integral
   $\sigma\cdot B$ of [[thm-localized-ito-integral]]. One writes
   $\displaystyle dX_t=b_t\,dt+\sigma_t\,dB_t$ for the display, and $b$ is
   called the **drift** and $\sigma$ the **diffusion coefficient** of this
   representation.

2. **Multidimensional Brownian-driven process.** Let $d\ge1$ and $m\ge1$ be
   finite integers, let $B=(B^1,\dots,B^m)$ be a standard $m$-dimensional
   Brownian motion [[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]] that is adapted to
   $(\mathcal F_t)$ and whose vector increment $B_t-B_s$ is independent of
   $\mathcal F_s$ for $0\le s<t$, let $X_0$ be a finite
   $\mathcal F_0$-measurable $\mathbb R^d$-valued random vector, let $b$ be an
   $\mathbb R^d$-valued progressively measurable process with
   $\int_0^t|b^i_s|\,ds<\infty$ almost surely for every $i$ and finite $t$, and let
   $\sigma=(\sigma^{ik})$ be an $\mathbb R^{d\times m}$-valued predictable
   process, each entry predictable
   [[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]], with
   $\int_0^t(\sigma^{ik}_s)^2\,ds<\infty$ almost surely for every $i,k$ and finite $t$.
   Then
   $$X^i_t=X^i_0+\int_0^tb^i_s\,ds+\sum_{k=1}^m\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s, \qquad i=1,\dots,d,$$
   defines an $\mathbb R^d$-valued **continuous Brownian Ito process** driven by
   $B$, using the progressive integral versions of [[thm-localized-ito-integral]]. Other progressive representatives agreeing on one measurable full event at every time represent the same process. No claim is made that an arbitrary null-path modification remains adapted.

The following well-definedness clauses are part of the definition and are used
throughout.

3. **The drift integral is a genuine pathwise integral.** Progressive
   measurability gives measurable sections and makes the positive and negative
   integrals $\mathcal F_t$-measurable by the parameter-integral part of Tonelli
   [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]], applied to Lebesgue measure on $[0,t]$ and the probability measure on $\mathcal F_t$.
   On the event where both extended integrals are finite, their difference is
   the drift integral; set it to zero otherwise. This is an adapted measurable
   convention, is finite everywhere, and on one probability-one event is
   absolutely continuous on every finite interval (take the countable
   intersection over integer horizons). It is progressive: the map
   $(t,\omega)\mapsto\int_0^tb_s(\omega)\,ds$, with the preceding finite-value
   convention, is measurable on every $[0,T]\times\Omega$ by parameter
   integration, and is adapted. Thus the definition uses the standard
   almost-sure drift and local-energy classes under the usual conditions.

4. **The stochastic integral exists, is unique and is continuous.** By
   [[def-locally-square-integrable-predictable-brownian-integrand]] and
   [[thm-localized-ito-integral]] the localized integral $\sigma\cdot B$ is a
   well-defined adapted process with continuous paths, unique up to
   indistinguishability, and each of its finite-energy pieces is a
   square-integrable martingale. The displayed integral representative is progressive; $X$ is adapted by its required progressive measurability and has
   continuous paths, $X_t$ is finite almost surely for each $t$, and
   $M^i_t:=\sum_k\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s$ is a continuous local
   martingale relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ in the sense of
   [[def-continuous-time-adapted-process-and-martingale]] for every $i$, with the common energy localizers described in clause 6.

5. **The coefficients are not part of the process.** A continuous Brownian Ito
   process may admit several representations $X=X_0+b\cdot\mathrm{Leb}
   +\sigma\cdot B$ with different pointwise representatives $(b,\sigma)$ (for example, altering a coefficient only at the single time zero), even for the same Brownian
   motion and filtration; this does not assert nonuniqueness of their equivalence classes modulo $\mathrm dt\otimes P$; conversely, two processes with the same displayed
   integral representation and the same $X_0$ are indistinguishable. Every
   statement on this page that mentions a decomposition uses only properties
   common to all representations of the given process. The separate
   quadratic-covariation definition that follows this item on its owning page
   is formulated from $X$ itself and not from $(b,\sigma)$; no
   quadratic-covariation definition is made inside this item.

6. **The class is closed under stopping and under linear combinations.**
   If $\tau$ is a stopping time, the literal stopped process $X^\tau$ is
   progressive. Indeed on $[0,T]\times\Omega$ the map
   $(t,\omega)\mapsto(t\wedge\tau(\omega),\omega)$ is measurable into
   $\mathcal B([0,T])\otimes\mathcal F_T$: the truncated time $\tau\wedge T$
   is $\mathcal F_T$-measurable, minimum is continuous, and rectangle inverse
   images give the assertion. Compose with the progressive restriction of $X$.
   Its drift is $b1_{[0,\tau]}$ and its diffusion is
   $\sigma1_{[0,\tau]}$; these retain almost-sure integrability and the required
   progressive/predictable measurability. The drift identity is pathwise.
   For the stochastic identity, apply the finite-energy stopping identity of
   [[thm-localized-ito-integral]], clause 4, on the canonical energy intervals
   of $\sigma$. The truncated integrand has finite energy on these same
   intervals. Comparing its canonical intervals with them at their pairwise
   minima by clause 4 identifies the localized integrals there. Countably
   many full-event agreements and exhaustion then give the identity at all
   times on one full event. Thus stopping closure uses localization, not a
   direct application of clause 4 to a possibly infinite-energy integrand.
   For finitely many coefficients, use the common continuous energy
   $E_t=\sum_{i,k}\int_0^t(\sigma^{ik}_s)^2ds$ and times
   $\kappa_n=\inf\{t:E_t\ge n\}\wedge n$, $n\ge1$.
   The same continuous-energy test as in the local-integrability definition
   makes these stopping times increasing to infinity almost surely, and bounds
   every stopped coefficient's expected energy by $n$. The preceding
   pairwise-minimum comparison shows that every integral stopped there is its
   finite-energy integral. Finite sums of these square-integrable martingales
   are martingales: finite sums preserve adaptation and integrability, and summing the integral test over any $A\in\mathcal F_s$ proves the conditional-expectation identity; hence their sums
   are local martingales with this common sequence. For fixed real constants,
   finite linear combinations of processes driven by the same vector Brownian
   motion have the combined coefficients. Their integrability follows from
   the triangle inequality and $(\sum_{j=1}^r u_j)^2\le r\sum_j u_j^2$.

7. **No pathwise integral against Brownian motion is defined.** The display
   defines the stochastic integral only as the localized limit of

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Induction in the recursion shows that $Y_k^h$ is $\mathcal F_{t_k}$-measurable: this holds for $Y_0=X_0$, and each update uses $\mathcal F_{t_k}$-measurable coefficients and a Brownian increment measurable at $t_{k+1}$. The interpolation is therefore adapted and continuous. For integration use the predictable step representative $\widehat Y_0^h=Y_0$ and $\widehat Y_s^h=Y_k^h$ on $(t_k,t_{k+1}]$; its coefficient processes $f(\widehat Y^h)$ and $g(\widehat Y^h)$ are predictable because each $Y_k^h$ is $\mathcal F_{t_k}$-measurable and $f,g$ are continuous. It agrees with $\bar Y^h$ outside the finite set of grid times. The recursion and interpolation give the same integral equation with these predictable coefficients. Setting $y=0$ in the coefficient inequalities yields $|f(x)|^2\le2|f(0)|^2+2D(1+|x|^q)|x|^2$ and $\|g(x)\|_F^2\le2\|g(0)\|_F^2+2c|x|^2$. The all-moment premise thus gives finite expected time-integral energy for these Euler coefficients; it gives the same for $f(X)$ and $g(X)$. The definition [F7] then makes the Euler interpolation and exact solution continuous Brownian Itô processes, and its linear-combination clause makes their difference $e$ one as well. In Itô's formula for $|e_t|^2$, the drift is $2\langle e_t,f(X_t)-f(\widehat Y_t^h)\rangle+\|G_t\|_F^2$ and the martingale term is $M_t=2\sum_{j=1}^m\int_0^t\langle e_s,G_{s,\cdot j}\rangle\,dW_s^j$, where $G_s=g(X_s)-g(\widehat Y_s^h)$. Since $e$ is continuous adapted and $G$ is predictable, each martingale integrand is predictable. Its finite expected energy follows from $\sum_j|2\langle e_s,G_{s,\cdot j}\rangle|^2\le4|e_s|^2\|G_s\|_F^2$ and $\mathbb E\int_0^T|e_s|^2\|G_s\|_F^2ds\le T(\mathbb E\sup_{s\le T}|e_s|^4)^{1/2}(\mathbb E\sup_{s\le T}\|G_s\|_F^4)^{1/2}<\infty$ by the all-moment and coefficient-growth premises.

Split the drift difference at $Y_t^h$. The one-sided Lipschitz bound and $2ab\le a^2+b^2$ give $2\langle e,f(X)-f(\widehat Y)\rangle \le(2\mu+1)|e|^2+|f(Y)-f(\widehat Y)|^2$ almost everywhere in time. The polynomial local-Lipschitz condition bounds the final term by $D(1+|Y|^q+|\widehat Y|^q)|Y-\widehat Y|^2$. Also, splitting $g(X)-g(\widehat Y)$ at $g(Y)$ and using its global Lipschitz bound gives $\|G\|_F^2\le2c|e|^2+2c|Y-\widehat Y|^2$. By [F2] with $r=2,4$, the all-moment premise, and [F5], $\mathbb E|Y_s-\widehat Y_s|^2\le C h$ and $\mathbb E\big[(1+|Y_s|^q+|\widehat Y_s|^q)|Y_s-\widehat Y_s|^2\big]\le C h$ for almost every $s$, uniformly in $h$. Thus the expected integrated drift is bounded by $C\int_0^t\mathbb E|e_s|^2\,ds+Ch$.

Apply [F4] to the vector integrand $K_s^j=2\langle e_s,G_{s,\cdot j}\rangle$. Since $\sum_j|K_s^j|^2\le4|e_s|^2\|G_s\|_F^2$, $\mathbb E\sup_{s\le t}|M_s| \le32\sqrt m\,\mathbb E\left[\sup_{s\le t}|e_s|\left(\int_0^t\|G_s\|_F^2ds\right)^{1/2}\right] \le32\sqrt m\left(v(t)\,\mathbb E\int_0^t\|G_s\|_F^2ds\right)^{1/2},$ where $v(t)=\mathbb E\sup_{s\le t}|e_s|^2$. From [F2] and the Lipschitz estimate for $g$, $\mathbb E\int_0^t\|G_s\|_F^2\,ds \le C\int_0^t\mathbb E|e_s|^2\,ds+Ch.$ Young's inequality therefore bounds the martingale term by $\frac12v(t)+C\int_0^t v(s)\,ds+Ch$.

Take the supremum over times up to $t$ in Itô's identity from step 1.1, take expectations, and insert the drift estimate from step 1.2 and martingale estimate from step 1.3. Moving $\frac12v(t)$ to the left gives $v(t)\le C\int_0^t v(s)\,ds+Ch.$ The all-moment assumption makes $v$ finite; pathwise continuity of $e$ and dominated convergence make $v$ continuous. Applying [F6] with the nondecreasing constant term $Ch$ yields $v(T)\le C'h$. The constants depend on $T,d,m,\mu,c,D,q$ and the all-moment bounds, but not on $h$.

Since $Y_T^h=Y_N^h$, the grid endpoint is included in the supremum bound. Taking square roots gives the stated root-mean-square order. AC is inherited exactly through [A1]; no choice principle is used in the numerical estimates.

citations.quote:
Use the data and grid of [[alg-euler-maruyama]], and let
$Y_0,\ldots,Y_N$ be its recursion. The left-endpoint map is
$$ \eta_h(t)=\max\{t_k:t_k\le t\},\qquad 0\le t\le T. $$
The right-continuous step process is
$$ \bar Y_t=Y_k\quad(t_k\le t<t_{k+1}),\qquad \bar Y_T=Y_N. $$
The continuous interpolation is the pathwise process
$$ Y_t=Y_k+b(t_k,Y_k)(t-t_k)+\sigma(t_k,Y_k)(W_t-W_{t_k})\quad(t_k\le t\le t_{k+1}). $$
At a shared grid endpoint the formulas agree because the recursion gives
$Y_{k+1}=Y_k+b(t_k,Y_k)h+\sigma(t_k,Y_k)(W_{t_{k+1}}-W_{t_k})$.
In particular $Y_{t_k}=Y_k$ for every $k$, including $Y_T=Y_N$.

For stochastic integration, define the predictable left-endpoint version by
$\bar Y^-_0=Y_0$ and $\bar Y^-_s=Y_k$ on $(t_k,t_{k+1}]$, and set
$\eta_h^-(0)=0$ and $\eta_h^-(s)=t_k$ on $(t_k,t_{k+1}]$. Its coefficient
integrands use the same fixed left endpoints. When the recursion is adapted,
each coordinate of $\bar Y^-$ and each coefficient composition is a
predictable finite-step process: on $(t_k,t_{k+1}]$ its value is
$\mathcal F_{t_k}$-measurable. These coefficients need not be bounded, so the
integrands need not be elementary in the bounded-coefficient sense of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Values at the finitely many
grid points do not change either integral. Once square integrability is
established, [[lem-square-integrable-predictable-step-ito-integral-is-finite-sum]]
identifies each finite-coordinate Itô integral of
[[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]] with its
finite-sum version, giving the equivalent formula
$$ Y_t=X_0+\int_0^t b(\eta_h^-(s),\bar Y^-_s)\,ds+\sum_{j=1}^m\int_0^t \sigma_{\cdot j}(\eta_h^-(s),\bar Y^-_s)\,dW_s^j. $$
where $\eta_h^-(s)=t_k$ on $(t_k,t_{k+1}]$ and
$\sigma_{\cdot j}$ denotes column $j$ of the matrix.

The justified-by theorem
[[thm-euler-maruyama-uniform-moment-and-increment-bounds]] establishes the
required integrability and well-definedness under the stated coefficient and
initial-moment conditions.

Assume the coefficient, filtered Brownian-motion, and initial-value
hypotheses of [[alg-euler-maruyama]] on a uniform grid with $0<h\le1$ and
$N=T/h\in\mathbb N$, with $\mathbb E|X_0|^p<\infty$ for a fixed finite
$p\ge2$. Let $Y_k$, $\bar Y$,
and $Y_t$ be the recursion, step process, and continuous interpolation of
[[def-euler-maruyama-step-process-and-continuous-interpolation]]. Then the
step process has a predictable representative, the interpolation formula
is well-defined, and $Y$ is adapted and continuous. There is a constant
$C_{p,T,L,K,d,m}$ independent of $h$ such that
$$ \max_{0\le k\le N}\mathbb E|Y_k|^p+\sup_{0\le t\le T}\mathbb E|\bar Y_t|^p+\sup_{0\le t\le T}\mathbb E|Y_t|^p\le C_{p,T,L,K,d,m}(1+\mathbb E|X_0|^p). $$
For every $t\in[0,T]$,
$$ \mathbb E|Y_t-\bar Y_t|^2\le C_{T,K,d,m}h(1+\mathbb E|X_0|^2). $$
These are pointwise-in-time moment bounds; no claim is made about
$\mathbb E\sup_{t\le T}|Y_t|^p$. The estimates hold under the shared
half-Hölder time-modulus contract, although this proof uses only the
uniform linear-growth bound and the Brownian increment assumptions.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let $H$ be a predictable
process on $[0,T]$, where $T\ge0$, with $E\int_0^TH_s^2ds<\infty$. Extend $H$ by zero after $T$ when applying the global continuous-version theorem, and let
$M_t=\int_0^tH_s\,dB_s$ be the continuous version of
[[thm-ito-integral-process-has-a-continuous-martingale-version]]. Then
$$E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|M_t|^2\le4\,E\int_0^TH_s^2\,ds .$$
The left-hand side is finite and does not depend on the chosen version, since
any two continuous versions are indistinguishable. Every continuous version of
the integral process satisfies the same bound. The path supremum in this
expectation means its measurable version $S_D=\sup_{q\in D}|M_q|$ on the
countable scaled dyadic grid $D$ (including both endpoints). Continuity
identifies it with the path supremum on a measurable event of probability one.
Indistinguishability here uses that full-event convention, as in the cited
continuous-version theorem, without assuming completeness of the filtration.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]: $B$ is a standard Brownian
motion on a filtered probability space, adapted to $(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$,
with $B_t-B_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ of law $N(0,t-s)$ for $0\le s<t$.
For this localized-calculus definition the filtration satisfies the usual
conditions, as required by
[[def-locally-square-integrable-predictable-brownian-integrand]].

1. **Real continuous Brownian Ito process.** A real progressively measurable process
   $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **continuous Brownian Ito process** when there are
   * a finite real $\mathcal F_0$-measurable $X_0$,
   * a real progressively measurable process $b=(b_s)_{s\ge0}$
     [[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]] with
     $\int_0^t|b_s|\,ds<\infty$ almost surely for every finite $t\ge0$, and
   * a real predictable process $\sigma=(\sigma_s)_{s\ge0}$, locally
     square-integrable in the sense that $\int_0^t\sigma_s^2\,ds<\infty$
     almost surely for every finite $t$
     [[def-locally-square-integrable-predictable-brownian-integrand]],

   such that, up to equality at all times on a measurable probability-one event,
   $$X_t=X_0+\int_0^tb_s\,ds+\int_0^t\sigma_s\,dB_s,\qquad t\ge0,$$
   where the first integral is the pathwise Lebesgue integral of $s\mapsto
   b_s(\omega)$ and the second is the localized Ito integral
   $\sigma\cdot B$ of [[thm-localized-ito-integral]]. One writes
   $\displaystyle dX_t=b_t\,dt+\sigma_t\,dB_t$ for the display, and $b$ is
   called the **drift** and $\sigma$ the **diffusion coefficient** of this
   representation.

2. **Multidimensional Brownian-driven process.** Let $d\ge1$ and $m\ge1$ be
   finite integers, let $B=(B^1,\dots,B^m)$ be a standard $m$-dimensional
   Brownian motion [[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]] that is adapted to
   $(\mathcal F_t)$ and whose vector increment $B_t-B_s$ is independent of
   $\mathcal F_s$ for $0\le s<t$, let $X_0$ be a finite
   $\mathcal F_0$-measurable $\mathbb R^d$-valued random vector, let $b$ be an
   $\mathbb R^d$-valued progressively measurable process with
   $\int_0^t|b^i_s|\,ds<\infty$ almost surely for every $i$ and finite $t$, and let
   $\sigma=(\sigma^{ik})$ be an $\mathbb R^{d\times m}$-valued predictable
   process, each entry predictable
   [[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]], with
   $\int_0^t(\sigma^{ik}_s)^2\,ds<\infty$ almost surely for every $i,k$ and finite $t$.
   Then
   $$X^i_t=X^i_0+\int_0^tb^i_s\,ds+\sum_{k=1}^m\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s, \qquad i=1,\dots,d,$$
   defines an $\mathbb R^d$-valued **continuous Brownian Ito process** driven by
   $B$, using the progressive integral versions of [[thm-localized-ito-integral]]. Other progressive representatives agreeing on one measurable full event at every time represent the same process. No claim is made that an arbitrary null-path modification remains adapted.

The following well-definedness clauses are part of the definition and are used
throughout.

3. **The drift integral is a genuine pathwise integral.** Progressive
   measurability gives measurable sections and makes the positive and negative
   integrals $\mathcal F_t$-measurable by the parameter-integral part of Tonelli
   [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]], applied to Lebesgue measure on $[0,t]$ and the probability measure on $\mathcal F_t$.
   On the event where both extended integrals are finite, their difference is
   the drift integral; set it to zero otherwise. This is an adapted measurable
   convention, is finite everywhere, and on one probability-one event is
   absolutely continuous on every finite interval (take the countable
   intersection over integer horizons). It is progressive: the map
   $(t,\omega)\mapsto\int_0^tb_s(\omega)\,ds$, with the preceding finite-value
   convention, is measurable on every $[0,T]\times\Omega$ by parameter
   integration, and is adapted. Thus the definition uses the standard
   almost-sure drift and local-energy classes under the usual conditions.

4. **The stochastic integral exists, is unique and is continuous.** By
   [[def-locally-square-integrable-predictable-brownian-integrand]] and
   [[thm-localized-ito-integral]] the localized integral $\sigma\cdot B$ is a
   well-defined adapted process with continuous paths, unique up to
   indistinguishability, and each of its finite-energy pieces is a
   square-integrable martingale. The displayed integral representative is progressive; $X$ is adapted by its required progressive measurability and has
   continuous paths, $X_t$ is finite almost surely for each $t$, and
   $M^i_t:=\sum_k\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s$ is a continuous local
   martingale relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ in the sense of
   [[def-continuous-time-adapted-process-and-martingale]] for every $i$, with the common energy localizers described in clause 6.

5. **The coefficients are not part of the process.** A continuous Brownian Ito
   process may admit several representations $X=X_0+b\cdot\mathrm{Leb}
   +\sigma\cdot B$ with different pointwise representatives $(b,\sigma)$ (for example, altering a coefficient only at the single time zero), even for the same Brownian
   motion and filtration; this does not assert nonuniqueness of their equivalence classes modulo $\mathrm dt\otimes P$; conversely, two processes with the same displayed
   integral representation and the same $X_0$ are indistinguishable. Every
   statement on this page that mentions a decomposition uses only properties
   common to all representations of the given process. The separate
   quadratic-covariation definition that follows this item on its owning page
   is formulated from $X$ itself and not from $(b,\sigma)$; no
   quadratic-covariation definition is made inside this item.

6. **The class is closed under stopping and under linear combinations.**
   If $\tau$ is a stopping time, the literal stopped process $X^\tau$ is
   progressive. Indeed on $[0,T]\times\Omega$ the map
   $(t,\omega)\mapsto(t\wedge\tau(\omega),\omega)$ is measurable into
   $\mathcal B([0,T])\otimes\mathcal F_T$: the truncated time $\tau\wedge T$
   is $\mathcal F_T$-measurable, minimum is continuous, and rectangle inverse
   images give the assertion. Compose with the progressive restriction of $X$.
   Its drift is $b1_{[0,\tau]}$ and its diffusion is
   $\sigma1_{[0,\tau]}$; these retain almost-sure integrability and the required
   progressive/predictable measurability. The drift identity is pathwise.
   For the stochastic identity, apply the finite-energy stopping identity of
   [[thm-localized-ito-integral]], clause 4, on the canonical energy intervals
   of $\sigma$. The truncated integrand has finite energy on these same
   intervals. Comparing its canonical intervals with them at their pairwise
   minima by clause 4 identifies the localized integrals there. Countably
   many full-event agreements and exhaustion then give the identity at all
   times on one full event. Thus stopping closure uses localization, not a
   direct application of clause 4 to a possibly infinite-energy integrand.
   For finitely many coefficients, use the common continuous energy
   $E_t=\sum_{i,k}\int_0^t(\sigma^{ik}_s)^2ds$ and times
   $\kappa_n=\inf\{t:E_t\ge n\}\wedge n$, $n\ge1$.
   The same continuous-energy test as in the local-integrability definition
   makes these stopping times increasing to infinity almost surely, and bounds
   every stopped coefficient's expected energy by $n$. The preceding
   pairwise-minimum comparison shows that every integral stopped there is its
   finite-energy integral. Finite sums of these square-integrable martingales
   are martingales: finite sums preserve adaptation and integrability, and summing the integral test over any $A\in\mathcal F_s$ proves the conditional-expectation identity; hence their sums
   are local martingales with this common sequence. For fixed real constants,
   finite linear combinations of processes driven by the same vector Brownian
   motion have the combined coefficients. Their integrability follows from
   the triangle inequality and $(\sum_{j=1}^r u_j)^2\le r\sum_j u_j^2$.

7. **No pathwise integral against Brownian motion is defined.** The display
   defines the stochastic integral only as the localized limit of
   [[thm-localized-ito-integral]]; no integral $\int_0^tH_s(\omega)\,dB_s(\omega)$
   along the individual path is asserted, and the page's examples show that
   the pathwise Riemann--Stieltjes route is unavailable.

the canonically localized integral is constructed in

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let $H$ be a locally
square-integrable predictable process
[[def-locally-square-integrable-predictable-brownian-integrand]] with localized
integral $H\cdot B$ in the progressively measurable version of
[[thm-localized-ito-integral]], with its measurable-full-event convention
for indistinguishability. The filtration satisfies the usual conditions and
local energy is finite almost surely on every finite horizon, as required by
the local-integrability definition. Let $\tau$ be a
stopping time [[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]]. Then the process
$s\mapsto(H\cdot B)_{s\wedge\tau}$ and the localized integral of the process
$1_{[0,\tau]}H$ are indistinguishable:
$$(H\cdot B)_{t\wedge\tau}=\int_0^t1_{[0,\tau]}(s)H_s\,dB_s\qquad\text{for every }t\ge0\text{, up to indistinguishability}.$$
In particular, for $H$ of finite energy this reduces to the stopping identity
of [[thm-localized-ito-integral]], and for $\tau\equiv\infty$ it is the
definition of the localized integral.

Let $t_0\le T$, let $u,a,b:[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $u,b\ge0$, and suppose

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t b(s)u(s)\,ds.$$

Then

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t a(s)b(s)\exp\!\left(\int_s^t b(r)\,dr\right)ds.$$

If $a$ is nondecreasing, this gives $u(t)\le a(t)\exp(\int_{t_0}^t b)$. The time-reflected form assumes $u(t)\le a(t)+\int_t^{t_0}b(s)u(s)\,ds$ for $t\le t_0$. In particular, when $a=A\ge0$ and $b=B\ge0$ are constant, the two orientations give $u(t)\le A e^{B|t-t_0|}$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice as required by the stochastic-integral interfaces
below. Fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$ and finite integers $d,m\ge1$. Work on
a complete filtered probability space
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{0\le t\le T},P)$ whose filtration is
right-continuous and contains every $P$-null subset of $\mathcal F$ in
$\mathcal F_0$ (the usual conditions).

Let $W=(W_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ be a standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion
[[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]] adapted to this filtration, with
$W_t-W_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and distributed as
$N_m(0,(t-s)I_m)$ for $0\le s<t\le T$. Let
$X_0:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$ be $\mathcal F_0$-measurable, satisfy
$E|X_0|^2<\infty$, and be independent of the future Brownian increments.
Explicitly, $X_0$ is independent of the sigma-algebra
$\sigma(W_t-W_0:0\le t\le T)$.

Continuity of a process means continuity on one measurable event of
probability one. We use an everywhere-continuous adapted representative: if
the chosen process is continuous only on such an event $A$, replace it off $A$
by its initial value. Since $A^c$ is a null set and the filtration is complete,
$A^c\in\mathcal F_0$; the replacement preserves adaptedness and changes the
SDE identity only on a null event, hence preserves it up to
indistinguishability.

The drift and diffusion coefficients are jointly Borel maps
$$b:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d,\qquad \sigma:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}.$$
For nonnegative finite constants $L,K$, assume for every $t\in[0,T]$ and
$x,y\in\mathbb R^d$ that
$$|b(t,x)-b(t,y)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(t,y)\|_F\le L|x-y|,$$
$$|b(t,x)|+\|\sigma(t,x)\|_F\le K(1+|x|).$$
Here $|\cdot|$ is the Euclidean norm and
$\|A\|_F^2=\sum_{i=1}^d\sum_{k=1}^m|A^{ik}|^2$ is the Frobenius norm.

For an adapted continuous candidate $X:[0,T]\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$,
the vector Itô equation
$$X_t=X_0+\int_0^t b(s,X_s)\,ds+\left(\sum_{k=1}^m\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}(s,X_s)\,dW_s^k\right)_{i=1}^d,\qquad 0\le t\le T.$$
uses a pathwise Lebesgue integral for the drift and, in each coordinate, the
localized Itô integral from
[[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]], clause 2. Require
$\int_0^T|b(s,X_s)|ds<\infty$ and
$\int_0^T\|\sigma(s,X_s)\|_F^2ds<\infty$ almost surely; these are the local
coefficient-integrability conditions in that definition. When a coordinate
integrand has finite expected energy, its integral is the square-integrable
Itô integral of [[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]];
the Picard estimates below establish that stronger condition for every input
in $\mathcal H_T$. Equality of processes means
equality for every $t$ on one measurable event of probability one, that is,
indistinguishability
[[def-law-modification-and-indistinguishability-of-processes]]. A **strong
solution on $[0,T]$** is an adapted continuous process satisfying this
integral equation indistinguishably. No moment bound is included in the
definition; the existence theorem proves its $L^2$ path-sup bound.
The usual-filtration, continuity, and finite-coordinate conventions agree
with the multidimensional class of continuous Brownian Itô processes
[[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]. This definition makes no ellipticity,
transition-density, forward-equation, or time-reversal assertion.

Assume the data and hypotheses of
[[def-ito-sde-and-strong-solution]] on $[0,T]$, with $T\ge0$, finite
dimensions $d,m\ge1$, Lipschitz constant $L$, and linear-growth constant
$K$. There is a strong solution $X$ on the given filtered probability space.
It is unique up to indistinguishability among strong solutions with the same
initial value and Brownian driver, and it satisfies
$$E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|X_t|^2\le(1+3E|X_0|^2)e^{C_TT},\qquad C_T:=6K^2T+24mK^2.$$
The bound is independent of any later numerical mesh.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space and let
$(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$ be a continuous-time filtration
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]].

1. A map $\tau:\Omega\to[0,\infty]$ (infinite values allowed) is a **stopping
   time** for $(\mathcal F_t)$ when
   $$\{\tau\le t\}\in\mathcal F_t\qquad\text{for every }t\ge0 .$$
2. For a stopping time $\tau$ its **stopped sigma-algebra** is
   $$\mathcal F_\tau:=\{A\in\mathcal F:A\cap\{\tau\le t\}\in\mathcal F_t \text{ for every }t\ge0\}.$$

The following facts are used below, and each is a direct set computation.

(a) $\mathcal F_\tau$ is a sigma-algebra: $\emptyset\cap\{\tau\le
    t\}=\emptyset\in\mathcal F_t$; for $A\in\mathcal F_\tau$ one has
    $A^c\cap\{\tau\le t\}=\{\tau\le t\}\setminus(A\cap\{\tau\le t\})\in\mathcal
    F_t$; and for a sequence $A_n\in\mathcal F_\tau$ the union satisfies
    $\bigl(\bigcup_nA_n\bigr)\cap\{\tau\le t\}=\bigcup_n(A_n\cap\{\tau\le
    t\})\in\mathcal F_t$. All operations are literal, not modulo null sets, and
    no completeness of the filtration is assumed.
(b) If $\tau\equiv t_0<\infty$ is deterministic, then
    $A\cap\{\tau\le t\}$ is $A$ for $t\ge t_0$ and $\emptyset$ for $t<t_0$, so
    $\mathcal F_\tau=\bigcap_{t\ge t_0}\mathcal F_t=\mathcal F_{t_0}$, where
    the last equality follows because the intersection includes its least
    member $\mathcal F_{t_0}$. If $\tau\equiv\infty$, then every test event
    $\{\tau\le t\}$ is empty and $\mathcal F_\tau=\mathcal F$.
(c) Suppose the filtration is right-continuous. Then $\tau$ is a stopping time
    if and only if $\{\tau<t\}\in\mathcal F_t$ for every $t>0$. Indeed
    $$\{\tau<t\}=\bigcup_{n\ge1}\{\tau\le t-\tfrac1n\}$$
    (with the terms for $t-\tfrac1n<0$ read as the empty set, since
    $\tau\ge0$), which gives the forward implication; conversely
    $$\{\tau\le t\}=\bigcap_{n\ge1}\{\tau<t+\tfrac1n\},$$
    and $\bigcap_n\mathcal F_{t+1/n}=\bigcap_{s>t}\mathcal F_s=\mathcal F_t$ by
    right-continuity together with monotonicity of the filtration.
(d) Under the same right-continuity assumption, for $A\in\mathcal F$ one has
    $A\in\mathcal F_\tau$ if and only if $A\cap\{\tau<t\}\in\mathcal F_t$ for
    every $t>0$: the forward implication follows from
    $A\cap\{\tau<t\}=\bigcup_n(A\cap\{\tau\le t-\tfrac1n\})$ and the converse
    from $A\cap\{\tau\le t\}=\bigcap_n(A\cap\{\tau<t+\tfrac1n\})$ together with
    $\bigcap_n\mathcal F_{t+1/n}=\mathcal F_t$.

Because the two versions of each test are interchangeable exactly when the
filtration is right-continuous, the convention is recorded here once: the
Brownian strong Markov theorem is stated for the usual augmentation, which is
right-continuous, and the raw-filtration statements use the non-strict test
directly. No choice principle is used by this definition.

The map $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[def-real-numbers]]) is an embedding of ordered
fields. Every real is approximated by rationals: for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and
rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with
$|x - \hat q| < \hat\varepsilon$. Consequently, strictly between any two
reals lies a rational.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: By [F4] and [F7], the exact process has its finite-coordinate Itô representation; [F1] supplies the Euler interpolation and its predictable representative $\bar Y^-$ with left-endpoint map $\eta_h^-$. Use that representative in the Euler integral form: $X_t=X_0+\int_0^t b(s,X_s)ds+\int_0^t\sigma(s,X_s)dW_s,$ $Y_t^h=X_0+\int_0^t b(\eta_h^-(s),\bar Y_s^-)ds+\int_0^t\sigma(\eta_h^-(s),\bar Y_s^-)dW_s.$ The grid-valued coefficients are predictable on $(t_k,t_{k+1}]$; their finite expected energy follows from the uniform pointwise second moments in [F2] and the linear-growth bounds, while the exact coefficients have finite energy by the stated $\mathbb E\sup|X|^2$ bound and the same growth condition. Thus these are the required integral representations. In subsequent estimates, $\bar Y$ and $\eta_h$ may replace their predictable versions because they differ only at finitely many grid times, which do not affect the integrals. For $R>0$ define $\tau_R=\inf\{t\le T:|e_t|\ge R\}\wedge T$, with $\inf\emptyset=\infty$. For $t<T$, $\{\tau_R\le t\}=\{\sup_{s\le t}|e_s|\ge R\}$, which is in $\mathcal F_t$ by continuity and [F9]; for $t\ge T$ the event is all of $\Omega$. Thus [F8] makes $\tau_R$ a stopping time. Subtracting the displays and using [F5] gives the stopped error as the sum of the two stopped coefficient integrals.

Put $\delta b_s=b(s,X_s)-b(\eta_h(s),\bar Y_s),\qquad \delta\sigma_s=\sigma(s,X_s)-\sigma(\eta_h(s),\bar Y_s).$ The state Lipschitz bounds, time modulus, and $|X_s-\bar Y_s|\le|e_s|+|Y_s^h-\bar Y_s|$ give $|\delta b_s|^2+\|\delta\sigma_s\|_F^2 \le C\left(|e_s|^2+|Y_s^h-\bar Y_s|^2+h(1+|\bar Y_s|^2)\right).$ Consequently, with $v_R(t)=\mathbb E\sup_{s\le t}|e_{s\wedge\tau_R}|^2$, [F2] bounds the expected drift-integrand error and the expected squared diffusion-integrand error, after stopping, by $C\int_0^t v_R(s)ds+Ch.$

Cauchy–Schwarz for time integrals bounds the squared supremum of the stopped drift integral by $T\int_0^t\mathbb E[1_{\{s\le\tau_R\}}|\delta b_s|^2]ds$. For the vector stochastic integral, write each state coordinate as a sum of the $m$ scalar Brownian integrals and use $|\sum_{j=1}^m z_j|^2\le m\sum_j|z_j|^2$. Applying [F3] to each scalar term yields the bound $4m\mathbb E\int_0^t1_{\{s\le\tau_R\}}\|\delta\sigma_s\|_F^2ds$. Using step 1.2 in both bounds gives $v_R(t)\le C\int_0^t v_R(s)ds+Ch,$ where $C$ is independent of $R$ and $h$.

The stopped error is bounded by $R$, so $v_R$ is finite and continuous; applying [F6] to step 2.1 gives $v_R(T)\le C_T h$ uniformly in $R$. Since $e$ is continuous on the compact interval, $\tau_R=T$ for all sufficiently large $R$ on each sample path. Taking $R=n\in\mathbb N$, the stopped suprema increase to $\sup_{s\le T}|e_s|^2$; monotone convergence [F11] yields $\mathbb E\sup_{t\le T}|e_t|^2\le C_T h$. Taking square roots gives the grid-point root-mean-square rate. AC enters only through [A1], and no arbitrary-index choice is used in the estimates.
