citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and use the finite-dimensional Brownian-motion
convention of [[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]]. Let the state dimension
$d$ and noise dimension $m$ be positive finite integers, and fix $T>0$ and
$N\in\mathbb N$ with $N\ge1$. Set $h=T/N>0$ and $t_k=kh$ for
$0\le k\le N$. Let
$b:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ and
$\sigma:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}$ be jointly Borel.
Write $|\cdot|$ for the Euclidean norm and $\|\cdot\|_F$ for the Frobenius
norm. Suppose finite constants $L,K$ satisfy, for every $s,t\in[0,T]$ and
$x,y\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$ |b(t,x)-b(t,y)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(t,y)\|_F\le L|x-y|, $$
$$ |b(t,x)|^2+\|\sigma(t,x)\|_F^2\le K^2(1+|x|^2), $$
and
$$ |b(t,x)-b(s,x)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(s,x)\|_F\le K(1+|x|)|t-s|^{1/2}. $$
Let $W$ be an adapted standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion on a filtered
probability space, with $W_t-W_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and law
$N_m(0,(t-s)I_m)$ whenever $0\le s<t\le T$. Let $X_0$ be
$\mathcal F_0$-measurable, independent of future Brownian increments, and
$\mathbb E|X_0|^2<\infty$.

The **Euler–Maruyama algorithm** takes these data as input and returns
$Y_0,\ldots,Y_N$:

1. Set $Y_0=X_0$.
2. For $k=0,\ldots,N-1$, form $\Delta W_k=W_{t_{k+1}}-W_{t_k}$ and set
   $$Y_{k+1}=Y_k+b(t_k,Y_k)h+\sigma(t_k,Y_k)\Delta W_k.$$

The output is the grid approximation for the coefficient pair $(b,\sigma)$.
The companion step-process and interpolation definition uses this same grid
and endpoint convention.

Use the data and grid of [[alg-euler-maruyama]], and let
$Y_0,\ldots,Y_N$ be its recursion. The left-endpoint map is
$$ \eta_h(t)=\max\{t_k:t_k\le t\},\qquad 0\le t\le T. $$
The right-continuous step process is
$$ \bar Y_t=Y_k\quad(t_k\le t<t_{k+1}),\qquad \bar Y_T=Y_N. $$
The continuous interpolation is the pathwise process
$$ Y_t=Y_k+b(t_k,Y_k)(t-t_k)+\sigma(t_k,Y_k)(W_t-W_{t_k})\quad(t_k\le t\le t_{k+1}). $$
At a shared grid endpoint the formulas agree because the recursion gives
$Y_{k+1}=Y_k+b(t_k,Y_k)h+\sigma(t_k,Y_k)(W_{t_{k+1}}-W_{t_k})$.
In particular $Y_{t_k}=Y_k$ for every $k$, including $Y_T=Y_N$.

For stochastic integration, define the predictable left-endpoint version by
$\bar Y^-_0=Y_0$ and $\bar Y^-_s=Y_k$ on $(t_k,t_{k+1}]$, and set
$\eta_h^-(0)=0$ and $\eta_h^-(s)=t_k$ on $(t_k,t_{k+1}]$. Its coefficient
integrands use the same fixed left endpoints. When the recursion is adapted,
each coordinate of $\bar Y^-$ and each coefficient composition is a
predictable finite-step process: on $(t_k,t_{k+1}]$ its value is
$\mathcal F_{t_k}$-measurable. These coefficients need not be bounded, so the
integrands need not be elementary in the bounded-coefficient sense of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Values at the finitely many
grid points do not change either integral. Once square integrability is
established, [[lem-square-integrable-predictable-step-ito-integral-is-finite-sum]]
identifies each finite-coordinate Itô integral of
[[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]] with its
finite-sum version, giving the equivalent formula
$$ Y_t=X_0+\int_0^t b(\eta_h^-(s),\bar Y^-_s)\,ds+\sum_{j=1}^m\int_0^t \sigma_{\cdot j}(\eta_h^-(s),\bar Y^-_s)\,dW_s^j. $$
where $\eta_h^-(s)=t_k$ on $(t_k,t_{k+1}]$ and
$\sigma_{\cdot j}$ denotes column $j$ of the matrix.

The justified-by theorem
[[thm-euler-maruyama-uniform-moment-and-increment-bounds]] establishes the
required integrability and well-definedness under the stated coefficient and
initial-moment conditions.

Assume the coefficient, filtered Brownian-motion, and initial-value
hypotheses of [[alg-euler-maruyama]] on a uniform grid with $0<h\le1$ and
$N=T/h\in\mathbb N$, with $\mathbb E|X_0|^p<\infty$ for a fixed finite
$p\ge2$. Let $Y_k$, $\bar Y$,
and $Y_t$ be the recursion, step process, and continuous interpolation of
[[def-euler-maruyama-step-process-and-continuous-interpolation]]. Then the
step process has a predictable representative, the interpolation formula
is well-defined, and $Y$ is adapted and continuous. There is a constant
$C_{p,T,L,K,d,m}$ independent of $h$ such that
$$ \max_{0\le k\le N}\mathbb E|Y_k|^p+\sup_{0\le t\le T}\mathbb E|\bar Y_t|^p+\sup_{0\le t\le T}\mathbb E|Y_t|^p\le C_{p,T,L,K,d,m}(1+\mathbb E|X_0|^p). $$
For every $t\in[0,T]$,
$$ \mathbb E|Y_t-\bar Y_t|^2\le C_{T,K,d,m}h(1+\mathbb E|X_0|^2). $$
These are pointwise-in-time moment bounds; no claim is made about
$\mathbb E\sup_{t\le T}|Y_t|^p$. The estimates hold under the shared
half-Hölder time-modulus contract, although this proof uses only the
uniform linear-growth bound and the Brownian increment assumptions.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and let $d\ge1$ be a finite integer. An
$\mathbb R^d$-valued process $B=(B_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **standard
$d$-dimensional Brownian motion** if:

1. $B_0=0$ almost surely;
2. for every finite list $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_n$, the vector increments
   $$B_{t_j}-B_{t_{j-1}},\qquad 1\le j\le n,$$
   are mutually independent and have laws
   $N_d(0,(t_j-t_{j-1})I_d)$; and
3. there is one measurable event $A$ with $P(A)=1$ such that
   $t\mapsto B_t(\omega)$ is continuous from $[0,\infty)$ to
   $\mathbb R^d$ for every $\omega\in A$.

Equivalently, its $d$ coordinate processes $B^\alpha=(B_t^\alpha)_{t\ge0}$
are independent standard one-dimensional Brownian motions. Here independence
of the processes means the following precise assertion. Put
$I=[0,\infty)$ and equip $\mathbb R^I$ with its cylinder sigma-algebra. The
maps
$$ \Phi_\alpha:\Omega\longrightarrow\mathbb R^I, \qquad \Phi_\alpha(\omega)(t)=B_t^\alpha(\omega), \qquad 1\le\alpha\le d, $$
are independent random elements.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. If $0\le s,t$ and a real random variable
$X_t-X_s$ has law $N(0,|t-s|)$, then, for every integer $m\ge1$,
$$E|X_t-X_s|^{2m}=c_m|t-s|^m,$$
where
$$c_m=E|Z|^{2m}=(2m-1)!!=1\cdot3\cdots(2m-1)<\infty$$
for $Z\sim N(0,1)$. In particular, when $m\ge2$, this is the moment hypothesis
of the one-parameter Kolmogorov criterion with
$\alpha=2m$, $\beta=m-1$, and $C_T=c_m$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let $m,d\ge1$ be finite
integers, let $B=(B^1,\dots,B^m)$ be a standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion,
and let $X$ be an $\mathbb R^d$-valued continuous Brownian Ito process
$$X^i_t=X^i_0+\int_0^tb^i_s\,ds+\sum_{k=1}^m\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s, \qquad i=1,\dots,d,$$
in the sense of [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]], including its usual-filtration and almost-sure coefficient-integrability conventions. Let
$f\in C^{1,2}([0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^d)$, meaning that $f,\partial_tf$,
$\partial_if$ and $\partial_i\partial_jf$ ($1\le i,j\le d$) exist and are
continuous. Then, up to indistinguishability, for every $t\ge0$
$$f(t,X_t)=f(0,X_0)+\int_0^t\Bigl(\partial_tf+\sum_ib^i\partial_if+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}\partial_i\partial_jf\Bigr)(s,X_s)\,ds+\sum_{i,k}\int_0^t\partial_if(s,X_s)\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s,$$
For the displayed integrands, intersect the measurable full events of continuity and the decomposition of $X$, and of coefficient integrability at all integer horizons. Its null complement belongs to $\mathcal F_0$ under the usual conditions. Set $X,X_0,b,\sigma$ to zero there. These representatives preserve all coefficient classes and the decomposition up to indistinguishability, with everywhere continuous $X$ and everywhere locally finite coefficient path integrals. All displayed integrands use these representatives.

The stochastic integrals are localized Ito integrals of the predictable
locally square-integrable integrands $\partial_if(\cdot,X)\sigma^{ik}$, and
$(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}_s=\sum_k\sigma^{ik}_s\sigma^{jk}_s$. In
differential form,
$df(t,X_t)=\bigl(\partial_tf+\sum_ib^i\partial_if+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}\partial_i\partial_jf\bigr)(t,X_t)\,dt+\sum_{i,k}\partial_if(t,X_t)\sigma^{ik}_t\,dB^k_t$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]: $B$ is a standard Brownian
motion on a filtered probability space, adapted to $(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$,
with $B_t-B_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ of law $N(0,t-s)$ for $0\le s<t$.
For this localized-calculus definition the filtration satisfies the usual
conditions, as required by
[[def-locally-square-integrable-predictable-brownian-integrand]].

1. **Real continuous Brownian Ito process.** A real progressively measurable process
   $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **continuous Brownian Ito process** when there are
   * a finite real $\mathcal F_0$-measurable $X_0$,
   * a real progressively measurable process $b=(b_s)_{s\ge0}$
     [[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]] with
     $\int_0^t|b_s|\,ds<\infty$ almost surely for every finite $t\ge0$, and
   * a real predictable process $\sigma=(\sigma_s)_{s\ge0}$, locally
     square-integrable in the sense that $\int_0^t\sigma_s^2\,ds<\infty$
     almost surely for every finite $t$
     [[def-locally-square-integrable-predictable-brownian-integrand]],

   such that, up to equality at all times on a measurable probability-one event,
   $$X_t=X_0+\int_0^tb_s\,ds+\int_0^t\sigma_s\,dB_s,\qquad t\ge0,$$
   where the first integral is the pathwise Lebesgue integral of $s\mapsto
   b_s(\omega)$ and the second is the localized Ito integral
   $\sigma\cdot B$ of [[thm-localized-ito-integral]]. One writes
   $\displaystyle dX_t=b_t\,dt+\sigma_t\,dB_t$ for the display, and $b$ is
   called the **drift** and $\sigma$ the **diffusion coefficient** of this
   representation.

2. **Multidimensional Brownian-driven process.** Let $d\ge1$ and $m\ge1$ be
   finite integers, let $B=(B^1,\dots,B^m)$ be a standard $m$-dimensional
   Brownian motion [[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]] that is adapted to
   $(\mathcal F_t)$ and whose vector increment $B_t-B_s$ is independent of
   $\mathcal F_s$ for $0\le s<t$, let $X_0$ be a finite
   $\mathcal F_0$-measurable $\mathbb R^d$-valued random vector, let $b$ be an
   $\mathbb R^d$-valued progressively measurable process with
   $\int_0^t|b^i_s|\,ds<\infty$ almost surely for every $i$ and finite $t$, and let
   $\sigma=(\sigma^{ik})$ be an $\mathbb R^{d\times m}$-valued predictable
   process, each entry predictable
   [[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]], with
   $\int_0^t(\sigma^{ik}_s)^2\,ds<\infty$ almost surely for every $i,k$ and finite $t$.
   Then
   $$X^i_t=X^i_0+\int_0^tb^i_s\,ds+\sum_{k=1}^m\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s, \qquad i=1,\dots,d,$$
   defines an $\mathbb R^d$-valued **continuous Brownian Ito process** driven by
   $B$, using the progressive integral versions of [[thm-localized-ito-integral]]. Other progressive representatives agreeing on one measurable full event at every time represent the same process. No claim is made that an arbitrary null-path modification remains adapted.

The following well-definedness clauses are part of the definition and are used
throughout.

3. **The drift integral is a genuine pathwise integral.** Progressive
   measurability gives measurable sections and makes the positive and negative
   integrals $\mathcal F_t$-measurable by the parameter-integral part of Tonelli
   [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]], applied to Lebesgue measure on $[0,t]$ and the probability measure on $\mathcal F_t$.
   On the event where both extended integrals are finite, their difference is
   the drift integral; set it to zero otherwise. This is an adapted measurable
   convention, is finite everywhere, and on one probability-one event is
   absolutely continuous on every finite interval (take the countable
   intersection over integer horizons). It is progressive: the map
   $(t,\omega)\mapsto\int_0^tb_s(\omega)\,ds$, with the preceding finite-value
   convention, is measurable on every $[0,T]\times\Omega$ by parameter
   integration, and is adapted. Thus the definition uses the standard
   almost-sure drift and local-energy classes under the usual conditions.

4. **The stochastic integral exists, is unique and is continuous.** By
   [[def-locally-square-integrable-predictable-brownian-integrand]] and
   [[thm-localized-ito-integral]] the localized integral $\sigma\cdot B$ is a
   well-defined adapted process with continuous paths, unique up to
   indistinguishability, and each of its finite-energy pieces is a
   square-integrable martingale. The displayed integral representative is progressive; $X$ is adapted by its required progressive measurability and has
   continuous paths, $X_t$ is finite almost surely for each $t$, and
   $M^i_t:=\sum_k\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s$ is a continuous local
   martingale relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ in the sense of
   [[def-continuous-time-adapted-process-and-martingale]] for every $i$, with the common energy localizers described in clause 6.

5. **The coefficients are not part of the process.** A continuous Brownian Ito
   process may admit several representations $X=X_0+b\cdot\mathrm{Leb}
   +\sigma\cdot B$ with different pointwise representatives $(b,\sigma)$ (for example, altering a coefficient only at the single time zero), even for the same Brownian
   motion and filtration; this does not assert nonuniqueness of their equivalence classes modulo $\mathrm dt\otimes P$; conversely, two processes with the same displayed
   integral representation and the same $X_0$ are indistinguishable. Every
   statement on this page that mentions a decomposition uses only properties
   common to all representations of the given process. The separate
   quadratic-covariation definition that follows this item on its owning page
   is formulated from $X$ itself and not from $(b,\sigma)$; no
   quadratic-covariation definition is made inside this item.

6. **The class is closed under stopping and under linear combinations.**
   If $\tau$ is a stopping time, the literal stopped process $X^\tau$ is
   progressive. Indeed on $[0,T]\times\Omega$ the map
   $(t,\omega)\mapsto(t\wedge\tau(\omega),\omega)$ is measurable into
   $\mathcal B([0,T])\otimes\mathcal F_T$: the truncated time $\tau\wedge T$
   is $\mathcal F_T$-measurable, minimum is continuous, and rectangle inverse
   images give the assertion. Compose with the progressive restriction of $X$.
   Its drift is $b1_{[0,\tau]}$ and its diffusion is
   $\sigma1_{[0,\tau]}$; these retain almost-sure integrability and the required
   progressive/predictable measurability. The drift identity is pathwise.
   For the stochastic identity, apply the finite-energy stopping identity of
   [[thm-localized-ito-integral]], clause 4, on the canonical energy intervals
   of $\sigma$. The truncated integrand has finite energy on these same
   intervals. Comparing its canonical intervals with them at their pairwise
   minima by clause 4 identifies the localized integrals there. Countably
   many full-event agreements and exhaustion then give the identity at all
   times on one full event. Thus stopping closure uses localization, not a
   direct application of clause 4 to a possibly infinite-energy integrand.
   For finitely many coefficients, use the common continuous energy
   $E_t=\sum_{i,k}\int_0^t(\sigma^{ik}_s)^2ds$ and times
   $\kappa_n=\inf\{t:E_t\ge n\}\wedge n$, $n\ge1$.
   The same continuous-energy test as in the local-integrability definition
   makes these stopping times increasing to infinity almost surely, and bounds
   every stopped coefficient's expected energy by $n$. The preceding
   pairwise-minimum comparison shows that every integral stopped there is its
   finite-energy integral. Finite sums of these square-integrable martingales
   are martingales: finite sums preserve adaptation and integrability, and summing the integral test over any $A\in\mathcal F_s$ proves the conditional-expectation identity; hence their sums
   are local martingales with this common sequence. For fixed real constants,
   finite linear combinations of processes driven by the same vector Brownian
   motion have the combined coefficients. Their integrability follows from
   the triangle inequality and $(\sum_{j=1}^r u_j)^2\le r\sum_j u_j^2$.

7. **No pathwise integral against Brownian motion is defined.** The display
   defines the stochastic integral only as the localized limit of
   [[thm-localized-ito-integral]]; no integral $\int_0^tH_s(\omega)\,dB_s(\omega)$
   along the individual path is asserted, and the page's examples show that
   the pathwise Riemann--Stieltjes route is unavailable.

Assume the data and hypotheses of
[[def-ito-sde-and-strong-solution]] on $[0,T]$, with $T\ge0$, finite
dimensions $d,m\ge1$, Lipschitz constant $L$, and linear-growth constant
$K$. There is a strong solution $X$ on the given filtered probability space.
It is unique up to indistinguishability among strong solutions with the same
initial value and Brownian driver, and it satisfies
$$E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|X_t|^2\le(1+3E|X_0|^2)e^{C_TT},\qquad C_T:=6K^2T+24mK^2.$$
The bound is independent of any later numerical mesh.

Assume the SDE data of [[def-ito-sde-and-strong-solution]] and the
global strong solution supplied by
[[thm-global-strong-well-posedness-for-lipschitz-ito-sdes]]. For every real
$p\ge2$ with $E|X_0|^p<\infty$, the unique solution satisfies
$$\sup_{0\le t\le T}E|X_t|^p\le 2^{p/2}(1+E|X_0|^p)e^{C_pT},\qquad C_p:=\sqrt2\,pK+p(p-1)K^2.$$
The supremum is over the individual-time moments; for $p>2$ this statement
does not assert an $E\sup_{t\le T}|X_t|^p$ bound. In particular, if $X_0$

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice and let $d\ge1$ be a finite integer. An
$\mathbb R^d$-valued process $B=(B_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **standard
$d$-dimensional Brownian motion** if:

1. $B_0=0$ almost surely;
2. for every finite list $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_n$, the vector increments
   $$B_{t_j}-B_{t_{j-1}},\qquad 1\le j\le n,$$
   are mutually independent and have laws
   $N_d(0,(t_j-t_{j-1})I_d)$; and
3. there is one measurable event $A$ with $P(A)=1$ such that
   $t\mapsto B_t(\omega)$ is continuous from $[0,\infty)$ to
   $\mathbb R^d$ for every $\omega\in A$.

Equivalently, its $d$ coordinate processes $B^\alpha=(B_t^\alpha)_{t\ge0}$
are independent standard one-dimensional Brownian motions. Here independence
of the processes means the following precise assertion. Put
$I=[0,\infty)$ and equip $\mathbb R^I$ with its cylinder sigma-algebra. The
maps
$$ \Phi_\alpha:\Omega\longrightarrow\mathbb R^I, \qquad \Phi_\alpha(\omega)(t)=B_t^\alpha(\omega), \qquad 1\le\alpha\le d, $$
are independent random elements.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: By [F6], the exact solution has the continuous Itô decomposition; apply [F5] to $u(t,X_t)$. The backward equation cancels its drift. Moreover, $|\nabla u(t,x)|\le C(1+|x|^q)$ and linear growth of $\sigma$ give $\mathbb E\int_0^T\|\nabla u(s,X_s)\sigma(s,X_s)\|_F^2ds<\infty$ because $p\ge2q+8$ and [F8] supplies the exact process moments. Thus the stochastic integral is a square-integrable mean-zero martingale by [F6]. With $u(T,\cdot)=\varphi$, this proves $\mathbb E\varphi(X_T)=\mathbb E u(0,X_0).$

Fix $t<T$, $x\in\mathbb R^d$, and $0<h\le\min(1,T-t)$; set $\Delta W\sim N_m(0,hI_m)$ and $\delta=b(t,x)h+\sigma(t,x)\Delta W$. Taylor's formula along the spatial segment gives $u(t,x+\delta)=\sum_{k=0}^3\frac1{k!}D_x^ku(t,x)[\delta^{\otimes k}]+R_4,$ $u_t(t,x+\delta)=\sum_{k=0}^2\frac1{k!}D_x^ku_t(t,x)[\delta^{\otimes k}]+R_3^t,$ where $D_x^ku[z^{\otimes k}]$ means the $k$th spatial derivative applied to $z$ in all $k$ slots. The integral remainders are $R_4=\frac1{3!}\int_0^1(1-r)^3D_x^4u(t,x+r\delta)[\delta^{\otimes4}]\,dr,$ $R_3^t=\frac1{2!}\int_0^1(1-r)^2D_x^3u_t(t,x+r\delta)[\delta^{\otimes3}]\,dr.$ Time Taylor expansion gives $u(t+h,x+\delta)=u(t,x+\delta)+hu_t(t,x+\delta)+R_{tt},\qquad R_{tt}=h^2\int_0^1(1-r)u_{tt}(t+rh,x+\delta)\,dr.$ The derivative bounds in the Statement and $|x+r\delta|^q\le C_q(|x|^q+|\delta|^q)$ imply $|R_4|\le C(1+|x|^q+|\delta|^q)|\delta|^4,\quad |R_3^t|\le C(1+|x|^q+|\delta|^q)|\delta|^3,\quad |R_{tt}|\le Ch^2(1+|x+\delta|^q).$ If $q=0$, interpret $1+|x|^q$ as the constant $2$.

For each finite real $s>0$, choose an integer $n\ge1$ with $2n\ge s$. If $Z$ is scalar standard normal, $|Z|^s\le1+|Z|^{2n}$, so [F4] gives $E|Z|^s\le1+(2n-1)!!<\infty$. For a standard $m$-dimensional Gaussian vector $G$, $|G|\le\sqrt m\max_j|G_j|$ gives $|G|^s\le m^{s/2}\sum_{j=1}^m|G_j|^s$, and hence $E|G|^s\le m^{1+s/2}\{1+(2n-1)!!\}$. By the Gaussian scaling convention in [F3] and [F9], $\Delta W$ has law $\sqrt h G$, so $E|\Delta W|^s\le C_{s,m}h^{s/2}$. This also covers $h=0$ when $s>0$; for $s=0$ adopt $|x|^0=1$, and its expectation is one. No initial-state moment stronger than the Statement is used in this Gaussian calculation.

The coefficient growth bounds and [F3]–[F4], [F9] give $\mathbb E\delta=b(t,x)h,\qquad \mathbb E(\delta\delta^{\mathsf T})=a(t,x)h+h^2b(t,x)b(t,x)^{\mathsf T},$ $\|\mathbb E(\delta^{\otimes3})\|\le Ch^2(1+|x|^3),\qquad \mathbb E|\delta|^s\le C_s h^{s/2}(1+|x|^s)$ for each finite exponent $s>0$ used in the Taylor remainders. Indeed, $|b(t,x)|+\|\sigma(t,x)\|_F\le C(1+|x|)$ and $|\delta|\le h|b(t,x)|+\|\sigma(t,x)\|_F|\Delta W|$; [F9] and $h\le1$ give the stated bound. When $q=0$, its $|\delta|^q$ factor is the constant $1$. For the third tensor moment, write $\delta=hb+Z$ with $Z=\sigma(t,x)\Delta W$. The centered Gaussian $Z$ has covariance $ha(t,x)$ and zero third moment, so expanding the tensor cube leaves three terms with one $hb$ and two $Z$ factors, plus $(hb)^{\otimes3}$; each has expectation $O(h^2(1+|x|^3))$. Substituting these moments in step 1.2, the first-order terms combine to $h(\partial_tu+b\cdot\nabla u+\frac12a:D_x^2u)(t,x)=0$. Every other Taylor term is bounded by $Ch^2(1+|x|^{q+4})$: the fourth spatial remainder uses $\mathbb E|\delta|^4(1+|x|^q+|\delta|^q)$, the time-space terms use $\mathbb E\delta$ and $\mathbb E\delta\delta^{\mathsf T}$, and the $u_t$ third-order remainder is $O(h^{5/2})(1+|x|^{q+3})\le Ch^2(1+|x|^{q+4})$. Therefore $\left|\mathbb E u(t+h,x+\delta)-u(t,x)\right| \le Ch^2(1+|x|^{q+4}).$

Condition on $\mathcal F_{t_k}$. By [F1], $Y_{k+1}^h$ is the one-step update in step 2.1 with $t=t_k$ and $x=Y_k^h$; [F3] makes the Brownian increment independent of $\mathcal F_{t_k}$. Thus $\left|\mathbb E\left[u(t_{k+1},Y_{k+1}^h)-u(t_k,Y_k^h)\mid\mathcal F_{t_k}\right]\right| \le Ch^2(1+|Y_k^h|^{q+4}).$ Since $p\ge2q+8\ge q+4$, [F2] and the exact pointwise moment premise make the expectation of the right side at most $C'h^2$, uniformly in $k,h$.

Sum the conditional one-step errors over $k=0,\dots,N-1$. The sum telescopes to $\left|\mathbb E u(T,Y_N^h)-\mathbb E u(0,Y_0^h)\right| \le NC'h^2=C'Th.$ Here $u(T,Y_N^h)=\varphi(Y_N^h)$ and $Y_0^h=X_0$; step 1.1 gives $\mathbb E u(0,X_0)=\mathbb E\varphi(X_T)$. Combining the equalities proves the desired weak error bound. AC enters only through [A1].

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d,m\ge1$ be finite, fix $T>0$, and work on
the complete usual filtered probability space of
[[def-ito-sde-and-strong-solution]]. Let $0<h\le1$ with $N=T/h\in\mathbb N$.
Use Euclidean state norms and the Frobenius matrix norm. Let $W$ be an adapted
standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion whose increments are independent of
the current filtration. Let
$b:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ and
$\sigma:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}$ be jointly Borel,
and suppose finite nonnegative constants $L,K$ satisfy, for all $s,t\in[0,T]$ and
$x,y\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$ |b(t,x)-b(t,y)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(t,y)\|_F\le L|x-y|, $$
$$ |b(t,x)|^2+\|\sigma(t,x)\|_F^2\le K^2(1+|x|^2), $$
and
$$ |b(t,x)-b(s,x)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(s,x)\|_F \le K(1+|x|)|t-s|^{1/2}. $$
Let $X_0$ be $\mathcal F_0$-measurable, independent of
$\sigma(W_t-W_0:0\le t\le T)$, with $\mathbb E|X_0|^2<\infty$. Let $X$ be the exact continuous
strong solution with
$$ \mathbb E\sup_{t\le T}|X_t|^2<\infty, $$
and let $Y^h,\bar Y^h$ be the continuous Euler interpolation and left-endpoint
step process of
[[def-euler-maruyama-step-process-and-continuous-interpolation]]. The
uniform pointwise moment and interpolation-increment bounds of
[[thm-euler-maruyama-uniform-moment-and-increment-bounds]] then imply that a
constant $C$, independent of $h$, satisfies
$$ \mathbb E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|X_t-Y_t^h|^2\le Ch. $$
Thus the grid-point root-mean-square error is $O(h^{1/2})$. The constant may
depend on $T,d,m,L,K$ and the exact-solution supremum-moment bound supplied by
the P-SDE-01 existence theorem.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d,m\ge1$ be finite, fix $T>0$, and work on
the complete usual filtered probability space of
[[def-ito-sde-and-strong-solution]]. Take $0<h\le1$ with $N=T/h\in\mathbb N$.
Let $W$ be an adapted standard
$m$-dimensional Brownian motion with increments independent of the current
filtration. Use Euclidean state norms and the Frobenius matrix norm, and write
$A:B=\operatorname{tr}(A^{\mathsf T}B)$. Let
$b:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ and
$\sigma:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}$ be jointly Borel,
globally Lipschitz in state, of uniform linear growth, and satisfy the
half-Hölder time modulus in [[alg-euler-maruyama]]. Let $X_0$ be
$\mathcal F_0$-measurable, independent of $\sigma(W_t-W_0:0\le t\le T)$, with
$\mathbb E|X_0|^p<\infty$ for some $p\ge2q+8$, where $q\ge0$ is finite;
when $q=0$, use the convention $|x|^q=1$.
Let $X$ be the exact strong solution and $Y^h,\bar Y^h$ the continuous
Euler interpolation and step process of
[[def-euler-maruyama-step-process-and-continuous-interpolation]].

For a bounded Borel payoff $\varphi:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$, define
$$ u(t,x)=\mathbb E\bigl[\varphi(X_T^{t,x})\bigr], $$
where $X^{t,x}$ is the unique shifted strong solution started from $x$ at time
$t$, supplied by [[thm-global-strong-well-posedness-for-lipschitz-ito-sdes]]. Set
$$ L_t v(x)=b(t,x)\cdot\nabla v(x)+\tfrac12\bigl(\sigma(t,x)\sigma(t,x)^{\mathsf T}\bigr):D_x^2v(x). $$
Assume $u(T,x)=\varphi(x)$ and $(\partial_t+L_t)u=0$ on
$[0,T)\times\mathbb R^d$. A multi-index is $\alpha=(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_d)$
with nonnegative integer entries and $|\alpha|=\sum_i\alpha_i$. Assume every
mixed derivative
$\partial_t^jD_x^\alpha u$ with $0\le j\le2$ and $|\alpha|\le4$ exists,
is continuous, and satisfies
$$ |\partial_t^jD_x^\alpha u(t,x)|\le C_u(1+|x|^q) $$
for a common constant $C_u$. Finally, assume the exact and Euler processes
have uniform pointwise moments of order $p$ on $[0,T]$; the Euler bounds are
provided by [[thm-euler-maruyama-uniform-moment-and-increment-bounds]] and the
exact bound by the P-SDE-01 moment contract. Then
$$ \bigl|\mathbb E\varphi(X_T)-\mathbb E\varphi(Y_N^h)\bigr|\le C h, $$
where $C$ is independent of $h$. The theorem is conditional on the stated
backward regularity; it does not derive that regularity from coefficient or
payoff smoothness.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that

derivations.claim: By [A1], the fine and coarse paths are driven by nested increments of this common Brownian path. Since $h\le1/M$, both meshes lie in the range of [F1]. Therefore $|Y_T^h-Y_T^{Mh}|^2 \le2|Y_T^h-X_T|^2+2|Y_T^{Mh}-X_T|^2.$ Taking expectations and applying [F1] at step sizes $h$ and $Mh$ gives $\mathbb E|Y_T^h-Y_T^{Mh}|^2\le2Ch+2CMh=2C(1+M)h.$ This is the correction second-moment bound.

The same Lipschitz bound and Cauchy–Schwarz give $|\mathbb E\varphi(X_T)-\mathbb E\varphi(Y_T^h)| \le L_\varphi\mathbb E|X_T-Y_T^h| \le L_\varphi\bigl(\mathbb E|X_T-Y_T^h|^2\bigr)^{1/2} \le C^{1/2}L_\varphi h^{1/2}.$ Thus $\beta=1$ and the strong route gives $\alpha=1/2$.

Let $D=\varphi(Y_T^h)-\varphi(Y_T^{Mh})$. Since variance is at most second moment and [A2] gives $|D|\le L_\varphi|Y_T^h-Y_T^{Mh}|$, step 1.1 yields $\operatorname{Var}(D)\le\mathbb E D^2\le2C(1+M)L_\varphi^2h.$

If the additional bounded-payoff backward contract holds, [F2] applied to the same fine Euler scheme gives bias at most $Ch$. It changes only the bias exponent to $\alpha=1$; the correction-variance bound of step 2.1 is unchanged.

A fine path takes $T/h$ Euler steps and the coarse path takes $T/(Mh)$ steps. The coarse increments are sums of already generated fine increments, so they add no Brownian draws; for fixed $M,d$ and unit-cost coefficient/payoff evaluations, total path work is proportional to $T/h+T/(Mh)=O(h^{-1})$. AC is inherited only through [A3].

Use the data and grid of [[alg-euler-maruyama]], and let
$Y_0,\ldots,Y_N$ be its recursion. The left-endpoint map is
$$ \eta_h(t)=\max\{t_k:t_k\le t\},\qquad 0\le t\le T. $$
The right-continuous step process is
$$ \bar Y_t=Y_k\quad(t_k\le t<t_{k+1}),\qquad \bar Y_T=Y_N. $$
The continuous interpolation is the pathwise process
$$ Y_t=Y_k+b(t_k,Y_k)(t-t_k)+\sigma(t_k,Y_k)(W_t-W_{t_k})\quad(t_k\le t\le t_{k+1}). $$
At a shared grid endpoint the formulas agree because the recursion gives
$Y_{k+1}=Y_k+b(t_k,Y_k)h+\sigma(t_k,Y_k)(W_{t_{k+1}}-W_{t_k})$.
In particular $Y_{t_k}=Y_k$ for every $k$, including $Y_T=Y_N$.

For stochastic integration, define the predictable left-endpoint version by
$\bar Y^-_0=Y_0$ and $\bar Y^-_s=Y_k$ on $(t_k,t_{k+1}]$, and set
$\eta_h^-(0)=0$ and $\eta_h^-(s)=t_k$ on $(t_k,t_{k+1}]$. Its coefficient
integrands use the same fixed left endpoints. When the recursion is adapted,
each coordinate of $\bar Y^-$ and each coefficient composition is a
predictable finite-step process: on $(t_k,t_{k+1}]$ its value is
$\mathcal F_{t_k}$-measurable. These coefficients need not be bounded, so the
integrands need not be elementary in the bounded-coefficient sense of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Values at the finitely many
grid points do not change either integral. Once square integrability is
established, [[lem-square-integrable-predictable-step-ito-integral-is-finite-sum]]
identifies each finite-coordinate Itô integral of
[[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]] with its
finite-sum version, giving the equivalent formula
$$ Y_t=X_0+\int_0^t b(\eta_h^-(s),\bar Y^-_s)\,ds+\sum_{j=1}^m\int_0^t \sigma_{\cdot j}(\eta_h^-(s),\bar Y^-_s)\,dW_s^j. $$
where $\eta_h^-(s)=t_k$ on $(t_k,t_{k+1}]$ and
$\sigma_{\cdot j}$ denotes column $j$ of the matrix.

The justified-by theorem
[[thm-euler-maruyama-uniform-moment-and-increment-bounds]] establishes the
required integrability and well-definedness under the stated coefficient and
initial-moment conditions.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let
$X_t=X_0+\int_0^tb_s\,ds+\int_0^t\sigma_s\,dB_s$ be a real continuous Brownian
Ito process [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]], under its usual-filtration
conditions, and let
$f\in C^{1,2}([0,\infty)\times\mathbb R)$, meaning that $f$, its first time
derivative $\partial_tf$ and its first two space derivatives
$\partial_xf,\partial^2_{x}f$ exist and are continuous on
$[0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$. Then, up to indistinguishability, for every
$t\ge0$
$$f(t,X_t)=f(0,X_0)+\int_0^t\Bigl(\partial_tf+b\,\partial_xf+\tfrac12\sigma^2\partial^2_xf\Bigr)(s,X_s)\,ds+\int_0^t\sigma_s\,\partial_xf(s,X_s)\,dB_s,$$
For the displayed integrands use the following representative convention.
Intersect the measurable full events of continuity of $X$, validity of its
decomposition, and local integrability of its coefficients at integer horizons.
Its complement is an $\mathcal F_0$-measurable null event by the usual
conditions. Replace $X,X_0,b,\sigma$ by zero there. This preserves the
decomposition up to indistinguishability and all coefficient classes, and
makes $X$ continuous everywhere and its coefficient path integrals locally
finite everywhere. All integrands below refer to these representatives.
The stochastic integral is the localized Ito integral of the predictable
locally square-integrable process $\sigma_s\partial_xf(s,X_s)$
[[thm-localized-ito-integral]] and the Lebesgue integral is the pathwise
integral of the progressively measurable process
$s\mapsto(\partial_tf+b\partial_xf+\tfrac12\sigma^2\partial^2_xf)(s,X_s)$,
which is pathwise integrable and finite almost surely for every $t$. In differential notation,
$df(t,X_t)=(\partial_tf+b\partial_xf+\tfrac12\sigma^2\partial^2_xf)(t,X_t)\,dt+\sigma_t\partial_xf(t,X_t)\,dB_t$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Fix $T>0$. For predictable
$H,K$ with finite energy $E\int_0^TH^2ds,E\int_0^TK^2ds<\infty$ the integrals
$\int_0^TH\,dB$ of
[[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]] satisfy
$$\int_0^T(H+K)\,dB=\int_0^TH\,dB+\int_0^TK\,dB,\qquad \int_0^T(aH)\,dB=a\int_0^TH\,dB\quad(a\in\mathbb R),$$
and the identities are equalities of $L^2(P)$-classes (almost sure
equalities). Moreover the map $H\mapsto\int_0^TH\,dB$ is an isometry,
$$E\Bigl(\int_0^TH\,dB\Bigr)^2=E\int_0^TH^2ds=\|H\|^2_{L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)},$$
it takes values in the mean-zero subspace of $L^2(P)$, and the bilinear cross
identity
$$E\Bigl[\Bigl(\int_0^TH\,dB\Bigr)\Bigl(\int_0^TK\,dB\Bigr)\Bigr]=E\int_0^TH_sK_s\,ds$$
holds for all such $H,K$. In particular the image of the map is a closed
subspace of $L^2(P)$ isometric to the predictable $L^2$ space of $H$'s, and
$H\mapsto\int_0^TH\,dB$ is injective up to the $(\mathrm dt\otimes P)$-class.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and work under the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]: a filtered probability space
with a standard Brownian motion $B$ adapted to the filtration, with increments
$B_t-B_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ of law $N(0,t-s)$. Fix $T>0$ and an
elementary predictable integrand
$$H_s=\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\xi_k\,1_{(t_k,t_{k+1}]}(s),\qquad 0=t_0<\cdots<t_m=T,$$
with bounded $\mathcal F_{t_k}$-measurable coefficients $\xi_k$. The **Ito
integral of $H$ against $B$** is the process
$$I_t(H):=\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\xi_k\bigl(B_{t\wedge t_{k+1}}-B_{t\wedge t_k}\bigr),\qquad 0\le t\le T,$$
also written $\int_0^tH_s\,dB_s$ or $(H\cdot B)_t$. The sum is finite and is
evaluated with the Brownian path of the given representative; on the event
where $t\mapsto B_t$ is continuous it is continuous in $t$, and $I_0(H)=0$
because $0\wedge t_k=0$ for every $k$.

Three conventions are part of the definition.

1. **Adaptedness and continuity.** For fixed $t$, each summand
   $\xi_k(B_{t\wedge t_{k+1}}-B_{t\wedge t_k})$ is $\mathcal F_t$-measurable:
   if $t<t_k$, the Brownian difference and hence the summand are zero; if
   $t\ge t_k$, then $\mathcal F_{t_k}\subseteq\mathcal F_t$, while
   $B_{t\wedge u}$ is $\mathcal F_t$-measurable for every $u$ because
   $t\wedge u\le t$. Thus
   $I(H)$ is adapted. For each fixed $\omega$ the map
   $t\mapsto B_{t\wedge t_{k+1}}(\omega)-B_{t\wedge t_k}(\omega)$ is continuous
   outside the single exceptional null set of (H) on which the Brownian path is
   discontinuous; the finite sum is therefore continuous on the same event.

2. **Linearity on a common refinement.** If $H$ and $K$ are elementary
   integrands and a partition refines both representations, then the defining
   sums of $H$, $K$, $H+K$ and $aH$ are taken over that common partition, and
   the finite sums give $I_t(H+K)=I_t(H)+I_t(K)$ and $I_t(aH)=aI_t(H)$ for real
   $a$ identically. In particular $I_t(H)-I_t(K)=I_t(H-K)$ for the
   elementary integrand $H-K$ represented on that refinement. This is a
   rearrangement of finitely many terms, not a limiting statement.

3. **Dependence on the representation is temporary.** The definition attaches
   $I_t(H)$ to a *chosen* elementary representation.
   [[lem-elementary-ito-integral-is-independent-of-the-step-representation]] proves that
   two representations that agree $(\mathrm dt\otimes P)$-almost everywhere
   produce the same random variables almost surely at each fixed time, so that
   $I_t(H)$ is a function of the $(\mathrm dt\otimes P)$-class of $H$ alone.
   Until then, every statement about an elementary integrand names the
   representation it uses.

The Axiom of Choice is declared because the standing hypothesis (H) is part of
the Brownian interface of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]], which assumes it; the
definition of the finite sum uses no choice. The countable-choice obligations
inherited from that interface are declared as dependencies of this item.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d,m\ge1$ be finite, fix $T>0$, and work on
the complete usual filtered probability space of
[[def-ito-sde-and-strong-solution]]. Let $0<h\le1$ with $N=T/h\in\mathbb N$.
Use Euclidean state norms and the Frobenius matrix norm. Let $W$ be an adapted
standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion whose increments are independent of
the current filtration. Let
$b:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ and
$\sigma:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}$ be jointly Borel,
and suppose finite nonnegative constants $L,K$ satisfy, for all $s,t\in[0,T]$ and
$x,y\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$ |b(t,x)-b(t,y)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(t,y)\|_F\le L|x-y|, $$
$$ |b(t,x)|^2+\|\sigma(t,x)\|_F^2\le K^2(1+|x|^2), $$
and
$$ |b(t,x)-b(s,x)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(s,x)\|_F \le K(1+|x|)|t-s|^{1/2}. $$
Let $X_0$ be $\mathcal F_0$-measurable, independent of
$\sigma(W_t-W_0:0\le t\le T)$, with $\mathbb E|X_0|^2<\infty$. Let $X$ be the exact continuous
strong solution with
$$ \mathbb E\sup_{t\le T}|X_t|^2<\infty, $$
and let $Y^h,\bar Y^h$ be the continuous Euler interpolation and left-endpoint
step process of
[[def-euler-maruyama-step-process-and-continuous-interpolation]]. The
uniform pointwise moment and interpolation-increment bounds of
[[thm-euler-maruyama-uniform-moment-and-increment-bounds]] then imply that a
constant $C$, independent of $h$, satisfies
$$ \mathbb E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|X_t-Y_t^h|^2\le Ch. $$
Thus the grid-point root-mean-square error is $O(h^{1/2})$. The constant may
depend on $T,d,m,L,K$ and the exact-solution supremum-moment bound supplied by
the P-SDE-01 existence theorem.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Here $b(x)=-x$ and $\sigma(x)=1$. Thus $|b(x)-b(y)|=|x-y|$, $|b(x)|^2+|\sigma(x)|^2=x^2+1$, and both coefficients are time independent. The initial value is square-integrable and independent of future Brownian increments, so the hypotheses of [F5] hold.
Apply [F2] to $F(t,x)=e^t x$ along $X$. Since $F_t+(-x)F_x+\frac12(1)^2F_{xx}=0$ and $F_x=e^t$, it follows that $e^tX_t=\int_0^t e^s dW_s$. At $t=1$ this gives $X_1=\int_0^1e^{-(1-s)}dW_s.$

The recursion is $Y_{k+1}=(1-h)Y_k+\Delta W_k$. Induction gives $Y_N=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}(1-h)^{N-1-k}\Delta W_k =\int_0^1(1-h)^{N-1-\lfloor s/h\rfloor}dW_s,$ where the second equality is [F4] on the grid partition.

By [F3] applied to the difference of the deterministic integrands, $\mathbb E|X_1-Y_N|^2 =\int_0^1\left|e^{-(1-s)}-(1-h)^{N-1-\lfloor s/h\rfloor}\right|^2ds.$ For $s\in[kh,(k+1)h]$, set $j=N-1-k$ and $u=s-kh$. Then $(1-s)=jh+(h-u)$, so $|e^{-(1-s)}-e^{-jh}|\le h$. Also $0\le e^{-jh}-(1-h)^j =e^{-jh}\left(1-e^{-j(-\log(1-h)-h)}\right) \le j(-\log(1-h)-h).$ For $h\le1/2$, the integral formula gives $0\le-\log(1-h)-h=\int_0^h\frac{x}{1-x}dx\le h^2$; since $j<1/h$, the last bound is at most $h$. Hence the integrand difference is at most $2h$ on every grid interval.

Integrating the bound of step 2.1 over $[0,1]$ gives $\mathbb E|X_1-Y_N|^2\le4h^2$, hence $(\mathbb E|X_1-Y_N|^2)^{1/2}\le2h$. This is a special additive-noise terminal rate; it is stronger than the general $O(h^{1/2})$ root-mean-square guarantee in [F5]. AC is inherited through [A1].

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let
$X_t=X_0+\int_0^tb_s\,ds+\int_0^t\sigma_s\,dB_s$ be a real continuous Brownian
Ito process [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]], under its usual-filtration
conditions, and let
$f\in C^{1,2}([0,\infty)\times\mathbb R)$, meaning that $f$, its first time
derivative $\partial_tf$ and its first two space derivatives
$\partial_xf,\partial^2_{x}f$ exist and are continuous on
$[0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$. Then, up to indistinguishability, for every
$t\ge0$
$$f(t,X_t)=f(0,X_0)+\int_0^t\Bigl(\partial_tf+b\,\partial_xf+\tfrac12\sigma^2\partial^2_xf\Bigr)(s,X_s)\,ds+\int_0^t\sigma_s\,\partial_xf(s,X_s)\,dB_s,$$
For the displayed integrands use the following representative convention.
Intersect the measurable full events of continuity of $X$, validity of its
decomposition, and local integrability of its coefficients at integer horizons.
Its complement is an $\mathcal F_0$-measurable null event by the usual
conditions. Replace $X,X_0,b,\sigma$ by zero there. This preserves the
decomposition up to indistinguishability and all coefficient classes, and
makes $X$ continuous everywhere and its coefficient path integrals locally
finite everywhere. All integrands below refer to these representatives.
The stochastic integral is the localized Ito integral of the predictable
locally square-integrable process $\sigma_s\partial_xf(s,X_s)$
[[thm-localized-ito-integral]] and the Lebesgue integral is the pathwise
integral of the progressively measurable process
$s\mapsto(\partial_tf+b\partial_xf+\tfrac12\sigma^2\partial^2_xf)(s,X_s)$,
which is pathwise integrable and finite almost surely for every $t$. In differential notation,
$df(t,X_t)=(\partial_tf+b\partial_xf+\tfrac12\sigma^2\partial^2_xf)(t,X_t)\,dt+\sigma_t\partial_xf(t,X_t)\,dB_t$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Fix $T>0$ and let
$h\in L^2[0,T]$ be deterministic, choose a Borel representative of its
Lebesgue-equivalence class, and set $h(s,\omega):=h(s)$. This process is
predictable with finite energy. Then the Ito integral
$\int_0^Th_s\,dB_s$
[[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]] is centered
normal with variance $\int_0^Th^2ds$: its law is $N(0,\int_0^Th^2ds)$ in the
convention of [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]], where $N(0,0)$ is the
Dirac law at $0$. More generally, for deterministic $h_1,\dots,h_d\in L^2[0,T]$
the vector of integrals is jointly Gaussian in the sense of
[[def-multivariate-normal-law]]: its law is $N_d(0,\Sigma)$ with
$$\Sigma_{jk}=\int_0^Th_j(s)h_k(s)\,ds .$$
In particular the covariance of the pair is
$\operatorname{Cov}(\int h_jdB,\int h_kdB)=\int h_jh_k$, the integrals are
uncorrelated exactly when $\int h_jh_k=0$, and integrals of deterministic
integrands with disjoint supports are independent.

Assume AC. If $X$ has law $N(m,\sigma^2)$ with $\sigma\ge0$, then $\varphi_X(t)=\exp(imt-\sigma^2t^2/2)$ for every real $t$. Moreover $\mathbb EX=m$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2$, including $\sigma=0$.

Use the data and grid of [[alg-euler-maruyama]], and let
$Y_0,\ldots,Y_N$ be its recursion. The left-endpoint map is
$$ \eta_h(t)=\max\{t_k:t_k\le t\},\qquad 0\le t\le T. $$
The right-continuous step process is
$$ \bar Y_t=Y_k\quad(t_k\le t<t_{k+1}),\qquad \bar Y_T=Y_N. $$
The continuous interpolation is the pathwise process
$$ Y_t=Y_k+b(t_k,Y_k)(t-t_k)+\sigma(t_k,Y_k)(W_t-W_{t_k})\quad(t_k\le t\le t_{k+1}). $$
At a shared grid endpoint the formulas agree because the recursion gives
$Y_{k+1}=Y_k+b(t_k,Y_k)h+\sigma(t_k,Y_k)(W_{t_{k+1}}-W_{t_k})$.
In particular $Y_{t_k}=Y_k$ for every $k$, including $Y_T=Y_N$.

For stochastic integration, define the predictable left-endpoint version by
$\bar Y^-_0=Y_0$ and $\bar Y^-_s=Y_k$ on $(t_k,t_{k+1}]$, and set
$\eta_h^-(0)=0$ and $\eta_h^-(s)=t_k$ on $(t_k,t_{k+1}]$. Its coefficient
integrands use the same fixed left endpoints. When the recursion is adapted,
each coordinate of $\bar Y^-$ and each coefficient composition is a
predictable finite-step process: on $(t_k,t_{k+1}]$ its value is
$\mathcal F_{t_k}$-measurable. These coefficients need not be bounded, so the
integrands need not be elementary in the bounded-coefficient sense of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Values at the finitely many
grid points do not change either integral. Once square integrability is
established, [[lem-square-integrable-predictable-step-ito-integral-is-finite-sum]]
identifies each finite-coordinate Itô integral of
[[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]] with its
finite-sum version, giving the equivalent formula
$$ Y_t=X_0+\int_0^t b(\eta_h^-(s),\bar Y^-_s)\,ds+\sum_{j=1}^m\int_0^t \sigma_{\cdot j}(\eta_h^-(s),\bar Y^-_s)\,dW_s^j. $$
where $\eta_h^-(s)=t_k$ on $(t_k,t_{k+1}]$ and
$\sigma_{\cdot j}$ denotes column $j$ of the matrix.

The justified-by theorem
[[thm-euler-maruyama-uniform-moment-and-increment-bounds]] establishes the
required integrability and well-definedness under the stated coefficient and
initial-moment conditions.

Assume the coefficient, filtered Brownian-motion, and initial-value
hypotheses of [[alg-euler-maruyama]] on a uniform grid with $0<h\le1$ and
$N=T/h\in\mathbb N$, with $\mathbb E|X_0|^p<\infty$ for a fixed finite
$p\ge2$. Let $Y_k$, $\bar Y$,
and $Y_t$ be the recursion, step process, and continuous interpolation of
[[def-euler-maruyama-step-process-and-continuous-interpolation]]. Then the
step process has a predictable representative, the interpolation formula
is well-defined, and $Y$ is adapted and continuous. There is a constant
$C_{p,T,L,K,d,m}$ independent of $h$ such that
$$ \max_{0\le k\le N}\mathbb E|Y_k|^p+\sup_{0\le t\le T}\mathbb E|\bar Y_t|^p+\sup_{0\le t\le T}\mathbb E|Y_t|^p\le C_{p,T,L,K,d,m}(1+\mathbb E|X_0|^p). $$
For every $t\in[0,T]$,
$$ \mathbb E|Y_t-\bar Y_t|^2\le C_{T,K,d,m}h(1+\mathbb E|X_0|^2). $$
These are pointwise-in-time moment bounds; no claim is made about
$\mathbb E\sup_{t\le T}|Y_t|^p$. The estimates hold under the shared
half-Hölder time-modulus contract, although this proof uses only the
uniform linear-growth bound and the Brownian increment assumptions.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. If $0\le s,t$ and a real random variable
$X_t-X_s$ has law $N(0,|t-s|)$, then, for every integer $m\ge1$,
$$E|X_t-X_s|^{2m}=c_m|t-s|^m,$$
where
$$c_m=E|Z|^{2m}=(2m-1)!!=1\cdot3\cdots(2m-1)<\infty$$
for $Z\sim N(0,1)$. In particular, when $m\ge2$, this is the moment hypothesis
of the one-parameter Kolmogorov criterion with
$\alpha=2m$, $\beta=m-1$, and $C_T=c_m$.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d,m\ge1$ be finite, fix $T>0$, and work on
the complete usual filtered probability space of
[[def-ito-sde-and-strong-solution]]. Take $0<h\le1$ with $N=T/h\in\mathbb N$.
Let $W$ be an adapted standard
$m$-dimensional Brownian motion with increments independent of the current
filtration. Use Euclidean state norms and the Frobenius matrix norm, and write
$A:B=\operatorname{tr}(A^{\mathsf T}B)$. Let
$b:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ and
$\sigma:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}$ be jointly Borel,
globally Lipschitz in state, of uniform linear growth, and satisfy the
half-Hölder time modulus in [[alg-euler-maruyama]]. Let $X_0$ be
$\mathcal F_0$-measurable, independent of $\sigma(W_t-W_0:0\le t\le T)$, with
$\mathbb E|X_0|^p<\infty$ for some $p\ge2q+8$, where $q\ge0$ is finite;
when $q=0$, use the convention $|x|^q=1$.
Let $X$ be the exact strong solution and $Y^h,\bar Y^h$ the continuous
Euler interpolation and step process of
[[def-euler-maruyama-step-process-and-continuous-interpolation]].

For a bounded Borel payoff $\varphi:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$, define
$$ u(t,x)=\mathbb E\bigl[\varphi(X_T^{t,x})\bigr], $$
where $X^{t,x}$ is the unique shifted strong solution started from $x$ at time
$t$, supplied by [[thm-global-strong-well-posedness-for-lipschitz-ito-sdes]]. Set
$$ L_t v(x)=b(t,x)\cdot\nabla v(x)+\tfrac12\bigl(\sigma(t,x)\sigma(t,x)^{\mathsf T}\bigr):D_x^2v(x). $$
Assume $u(T,x)=\varphi(x)$ and $(\partial_t+L_t)u=0$ on
$[0,T)\times\mathbb R^d$. A multi-index is $\alpha=(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_d)$
with nonnegative integer entries and $|\alpha|=\sum_i\alpha_i$. Assume every
mixed derivative
$\partial_t^jD_x^\alpha u$ with $0\le j\le2$ and $|\alpha|\le4$ exists,
is continuous, and satisfies
$$ |\partial_t^jD_x^\alpha u(t,x)|\le C_u(1+|x|^q) $$
for a common constant $C_u$. Finally, assume the exact and Euler processes
have uniform pointwise moments of order $p$ on $[0,T]$; the Euler bounds are
provided by [[thm-euler-maruyama-uniform-moment-and-increment-bounds]] and the
exact bound by the P-SDE-01 moment contract. Then
$$ \bigl|\mathbb E\varphi(X_T)-\mathbb E\varphi(Y_N^h)\bigr|\le C h, $$
where $C$ is independent of $h$. The theorem is conditional on the stated
backward regularity; it does not derive that regularity from coefficient or
payoff smoothness.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Apply [F1] to $e^tX_t$. The drift terms cancel, so $X_t=\int_0^t e^{-(t-s)}dW_s.$ For a solution started at $(t,x)$, the same calculation gives $X_1^{t,x}=r(t)x+\int_t^1 e^{-(1-s)}dW_s.$ By [F2], the last integral is $N(0,(1-r(t)^2)/2)$.

Since $r'=r$ and $A(t):=e^{-(1-r(t)^2)/4}$ satisfies $A'/A=r^2/2$, direct differentiation gives $u_t=A\left(\frac{r^2}{2}\cos(rx)-rx\sin(rx)\right), \qquad u_x=-Ar\sin(rx), \qquad u_{xx}=-Ar^2\cos(rx).$ For the generator $L=-x\partial_x+\frac12\partial_{xx}$, these formulas imply $(\partial_t+L)u=0$. Every mixed derivative $\partial_t^j\partial_x^ku$ with $j\le2$, $k\le4$ is a finite sum of bounded smooth coefficient functions times $x^a\sin(rx)$ or $x^a\cos(rx)$ with $a\le2$; hence it is bounded by $C(1+|x|^2)$. The backward contract holds with $q=2$.

By [F3], for that normal variable $Z$, $\mathbb E e^{iZ}=e^{-(1-r^2)/4}$. Taking the real part after multiplying by $e^{irx}$ gives $\mathbb E\cos(X_1^{t,x}) =e^{-(1-r(t)^2)/4}\cos(r(t)x)=u(t,x).$ Thus $u$ is the stated backward value function and $u(1,x)=\cos x$.

The exact process is centered normal at each time with variance $(1-e^{-2t})/2\le1/2$ by [F2], so [F6] at order $12$ gives $E|X_t|^{12}=11!!\{(1-e^{-2t})/2\}^6\le11!!/64$ uniformly in $t\in[0,1]$, including $t=0$. For the Euler process, $b(x)=-x$ is globally Lipschitz with linear growth, $\sigma(x)=1$ is globally Lipschitz with linear growth, the time modulus is zero, and $X_0=0$ has every moment. Applying [F5] at $p=12$ therefore gives uniform pointwise 12th moments for $Y^h$ and $\bar Y^h$. The threshold is $p=12=2q+8$.

The payoff is bounded and $1$-Lipschitz. By [F4], the interpolation agrees with the Euler recursion at $T$, so the conclusion of [F7] applies to $Y_N^h$. Steps 2.1–2.2 verify its backward regularity and moment premises, giving $|\mathbb E\cos(X_1)-\mathbb E\cos(Y_N^h)|\le Ch$. AC is inherited through [A1].

Assume the Axiom of Choice and let $d\ge1$ be a finite integer. An
$\mathbb R^d$-valued process $B=(B_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **standard
$d$-dimensional Brownian motion** if:

1. $B_0=0$ almost surely;
2. for every finite list $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_n$, the vector increments
   $$B_{t_j}-B_{t_{j-1}},\qquad 1\le j\le n,$$
   are mutually independent and have laws
   $N_d(0,(t_j-t_{j-1})I_d)$; and
3. there is one measurable event $A$ with $P(A)=1$ such that
   $t\mapsto B_t(\omega)$ is continuous from $[0,\infty)$ to
   $\mathbb R^d$ for every $\omega\in A$.

Equivalently, its $d$ coordinate processes $B^\alpha=(B_t^\alpha)_{t\ge0}$
are independent standard one-dimensional Brownian motions. Here independence
of the processes means the following precise assertion. Put
$I=[0,\infty)$ and equip $\mathbb R^I$ with its cylinder sigma-algebra. The
maps
$$ \Phi_\alpha:\Omega\longrightarrow\mathbb R^I, \qquad \Phi_\alpha(\omega)(t)=B_t^\alpha(\omega), \qquad 1\le\alpha\le d, $$
are independent random elements.

Assume AC. If $X$ has law $N(m,\sigma^2)$ with $\sigma\ge0$, then $\varphi_X(t)=\exp(imt-\sigma^2t^2/2)$ for every real $t$. Moreover $\mathbb EX=m$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2$, including $\sigma=0$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and use the finite-dimensional Brownian-motion
convention of [[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]]. Let the state dimension
$d$ and noise dimension $m$ be positive finite integers, and fix $T>0$ and
$N\in\mathbb N$ with $N\ge1$. Set $h=T/N>0$ and $t_k=kh$ for
$0\le k\le N$. Let
$b:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ and
$\sigma:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}$ be jointly Borel.
Write $|\cdot|$ for the Euclidean norm and $\|\cdot\|_F$ for the Frobenius
norm. Suppose finite constants $L,K$ satisfy, for every $s,t\in[0,T]$ and
$x,y\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$ |b(t,x)-b(t,y)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(t,y)\|_F\le L|x-y|, $$
$$ |b(t,x)|^2+\|\sigma(t,x)\|_F^2\le K^2(1+|x|^2), $$
and
$$ |b(t,x)-b(s,x)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(s,x)\|_F\le K(1+|x|)|t-s|^{1/2}. $$
Let $W$ be an adapted standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion on a filtered
probability space, with $W_t-W_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and law
$N_m(0,(t-s)I_m)$ whenever $0\le s<t\le T$. Let $X_0$ be
$\mathcal F_0$-measurable, independent of future Brownian increments, and
$\mathbb E|X_0|^2<\infty$.

The **Euler–Maruyama algorithm** takes these data as input and returns
$Y_0,\ldots,Y_N$:

1. Set $Y_0=X_0$.
2. For $k=0,\ldots,N-1$, form $\Delta W_k=W_{t_{k+1}}-W_{t_k}$ and set
   $$Y_{k+1}=Y_k+b(t_k,Y_k)h+\sigma(t_k,Y_k)\Delta W_k.$$

The output is the grid approximation for the coefficient pair $(b,\sigma)$.
The companion step-process and interpolation definition uses this same grid
and endpoint convention.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d,m\ge1$ be finite, fix $T>0$, and work on
the complete usual filtered probability space of
[[def-ito-sde-and-strong-solution]]. Let $0<h\le1$ with $N=T/h\in\mathbb N$.
Use Euclidean state norms and the Frobenius matrix norm. Let $W$ be an adapted
standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion whose increments are independent of
the current filtration. Let
$b:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ and
$\sigma:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}$ be jointly Borel,
and suppose finite nonnegative constants $L,K$ satisfy, for all $s,t\in[0,T]$ and
$x,y\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$ |b(t,x)-b(t,y)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(t,y)\|_F\le L|x-y|, $$
$$ |b(t,x)|^2+\|\sigma(t,x)\|_F^2\le K^2(1+|x|^2), $$
and
$$ |b(t,x)-b(s,x)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(s,x)\|_F \le K(1+|x|)|t-s|^{1/2}. $$
Let $X_0$ be $\mathcal F_0$-measurable, independent of
$\sigma(W_t-W_0:0\le t\le T)$, with $\mathbb E|X_0|^2<\infty$. Let $X$ be the exact continuous
strong solution with
$$ \mathbb E\sup_{t\le T}|X_t|^2<\infty, $$
and let $Y^h,\bar Y^h$ be the continuous Euler interpolation and left-endpoint
step process of
[[def-euler-maruyama-step-process-and-continuous-interpolation]]. The
uniform pointwise moment and interpolation-increment bounds of
[[thm-euler-maruyama-uniform-moment-and-increment-bounds]] then imply that a
constant $C$, independent of $h$, satisfies
$$ \mathbb E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|X_t-Y_t^h|^2\le Ch. $$
Thus the grid-point root-mean-square error is $O(h^{1/2})$. The constant may
depend on $T,d,m,L,K$ and the exact-solution supremum-moment bound supplied by
the P-SDE-01 existence theorem.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: The target equation has terminal value $X_1=W_1$. By [F1]–[F2], $\mathbb E\cos(X_1)=\operatorname{Re}\mathbb E e^{iW_1}=e^{-1/2}.$ The learned Euler recursion is $\widehat Y_{k+1}=\widehat Y_k+(\pi/2)h+\Delta W_k$. Summing its $N$ increments gives $\widehat Y_N=\frac\pi2 Nh+\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\Delta W_k=\frac\pi2+W_1,$ which is exactly $\widehat X_1$ for every $h=1/N$. Thus the discretization error relative to the learned equation is zero.

By [F2] and the addition formula, $\mathbb E\cos(\widehat X_1) =\operatorname{Re}\left(e^{i\pi/2}\mathbb E e^{iW_1}\right)=0.$ Therefore the absolute expectation bias relative to the target is $|0-e^{-1/2}|=e^{-1/2}>0$ for every step size, so it persists as $h\to0$. The solver theorem [F4] controls error to the learned SDE solution; it supplies no bound on the difference between the learned and target drifts. AC is inherited through [A1].

Example fixes X_0=hat X_0=0 deterministically and sigma=1, and the exact constant learned drift pi/2 makes the solver terminal value exact.
Verification step 1.1 sums N increments over [0,1] to W_1; the step-size limit in step 2.1 preserves the positive bias instead of removing it.
Verification step 2.1 explicitly attributes AC to A1 and the normal characteristic-function interface; neither model nor its coupling is selected from a family.

finite_checks.claim: For N=2, Euler is exact for the constant learned drift and the cosine payoff bias relative to the target is e^(−1/2).
finite_checks.result: Summing two updates gives Yhat2=π/2+W1. The target cosine mean is e^(−1/2), while the learned cosine mean is Re(i e^(−1/2))=0; the absolute bias is e^(−1/2)>0.

Assume AC and the finite-$L^2$ coefficient and initial-value hypotheses of
[[thm-euler-maruyama-strong-rate-for-square-integrable-initial-data]]. Fix an
integer refinement factor $M\ge2$ and a fine step $h$ with $0<h\le1/M$,
$T/h\in\mathbb N$, and $T/(Mh)\in\mathbb N$. Construct the fine and coarse
Euler paths with the same initial value and Brownian motion. The coarse
Brownian increment over each coarse interval is, by definition, the sum of
the $M$ fine Brownian increments in that interval. Let $X_T$ be the common
exact solution, and let $\varphi:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be globally
Lipschitz with constant $L_\varphi$. Then constants independent of $h$ satisfy
$$ \mathbb E|Y_T^h-Y_T^{Mh}|^2\le C_M h, $$
$$ \operatorname{Var}\bigl(\varphi(Y_T^h)-\varphi(Y_T^{Mh})\bigr)\le C_ML_\varphi^2h, \qquad |\mathbb E\varphi(X_T)-\mathbb E\varphi(Y_T^h)|\le C L_\varphi h^{1/2}. $$
Thus the Lipschitz-payoff Euler level pair has correction variance exponent
$\beta=1$ and strong-error bias exponent $\alpha=1/2$. If, in addition,
$\varphi$ is bounded and its backward value function satisfies the hypotheses
of [[thm-euler-maruyama-weak-order-one-under-backward-regularity]], then the
bias bound improves to $|\mathbb E\varphi(X_T)-\mathbb E\varphi(Y_T^h)|\le Ch$,
so $\alpha=1$ while $\beta=1$ remains. With fixed dimension, fixed $M$, and
unit-cost coefficient and payoff evaluations, one coupled fine/coarse sample
has work $O(h^{-1})$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let
$X_t=X_0+\int_0^tb_s\,ds+\int_0^t\sigma_s\,dB_s$ be a real continuous Brownian
Ito process [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]], under its usual-filtration
conditions, and let
$f\in C^{1,2}([0,\infty)\times\mathbb R)$, meaning that $f$, its first time
derivative $\partial_tf$ and its first two space derivatives
$\partial_xf,\partial^2_{x}f$ exist and are continuous on
$[0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$. Then, up to indistinguishability, for every
$t\ge0$
$$f(t,X_t)=f(0,X_0)+\int_0^t\Bigl(\partial_tf+b\,\partial_xf+\tfrac12\sigma^2\partial^2_xf\Bigr)(s,X_s)\,ds+\int_0^t\sigma_s\,\partial_xf(s,X_s)\,dB_s,$$
For the displayed integrands use the following representative convention.
Intersect the measurable full events of continuity of $X$, validity of its
decomposition, and local integrability of its coefficients at integer horizons.
Its complement is an $\mathcal F_0$-measurable null event by the usual
conditions. Replace $X,X_0,b,\sigma$ by zero there. This preserves the
decomposition up to indistinguishability and all coefficient classes, and
makes $X$ continuous everywhere and its coefficient path integrals locally
finite everywhere. All integrands below refer to these representatives.
The stochastic integral is the localized Ito integral of the predictable
locally square-integrable process $\sigma_s\partial_xf(s,X_s)$
[[thm-localized-ito-integral]] and the Lebesgue integral is the pathwise
integral of the progressively measurable process
$s\mapsto(\partial_tf+b\partial_xf+\tfrac12\sigma^2\partial^2_xf)(s,X_s)$,
which is pathwise integrable and finite almost surely for every $t$. In differential notation,
$df(t,X_t)=(\partial_tf+b\partial_xf+\tfrac12\sigma^2\partial^2_xf)(t,X_t)\,dt+\sigma_t\partial_xf(t,X_t)\,dB_t$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let $H$ be a predictable
process on $[0,T]$, where $T\ge0$, with $E\int_0^TH_s^2ds<\infty$. Extend $H$ by zero after $T$ when applying the global continuous-version theorem, and let
$M_t=\int_0^tH_s\,dB_s$ be the continuous version of
[[thm-ito-integral-process-has-a-continuous-martingale-version]]. Then
$$E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|M_t|^2\le4\,E\int_0^TH_s^2\,ds .$$
The left-hand side is finite and does not depend on the chosen version, since
any two continuous versions are indistinguishable. Every continuous version of
the integral process satisfies the same bound. The path supremum in this
expectation means its measurable version $S_D=\sup_{q\in D}|M_q|$ on the
countable scaled dyadic grid $D$ (including both endpoints). Continuity
identifies it with the path supremum on a measurable event of probability one.
Indistinguishability here uses that full-event convention, as in the cited
continuous-version theorem, without assuming completeness of the filtration.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and let $d\ge1$ be a finite integer. An
$\mathbb R^d$-valued process $B=(B_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **standard
$d$-dimensional Brownian motion** if:

1. $B_0=0$ almost surely;
2. for every finite list $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_n$, the vector increments
   $$B_{t_j}-B_{t_{j-1}},\qquad 1\le j\le n,$$
   are mutually independent and have laws
   $N_d(0,(t_j-t_{j-1})I_d)$; and
3. there is one measurable event $A$ with $P(A)=1$ such that
   $t\mapsto B_t(\omega)$ is continuous from $[0,\infty)$ to
   $\mathbb R^d$ for every $\omega\in A$.

Equivalently, its $d$ coordinate processes $B^\alpha=(B_t^\alpha)_{t\ge0}$
are independent standard one-dimensional Brownian motions. Here independence
of the processes means the following precise assertion. Put
$I=[0,\infty)$ and equip $\mathbb R^I$ with its cylinder sigma-algebra. The
maps
$$ \Phi_\alpha:\Omega\longrightarrow\mathbb R^I, \qquad \Phi_\alpha(\omega)(t)=B_t^\alpha(\omega), \qquad 1\le\alpha\le d, $$
are independent random elements.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if

Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that

derivations.claim: The coefficients are $b(x)=-x$ and $\sigma(x)=1$. They are globally Lipschitz with constant $1$, satisfy $|b(x)|^2+|\sigma(x)|^2=x^2+1$, and are time independent, so the shared coefficient and time-modulus conditions hold. Applying [F2] to $e^tX_t$ gives $X_t=e^{-t}\int_0^t e^s dW_s$. Applying [F2] to $e^tW_t$ then gives $X_t=\int_0^t e^{-(t-s)}dW_s =W_t-\int_0^t e^{-(t-s)}W_sds.$ Hence $\sup_{t\le1}|X_t|\le2\sup_{t\le1}|W_t|$, and [F3] gives $\mathbb E\sup_{t\le1}|X_t|^2\le16<\infty$.

The payoff satisfies [A2]. The fine and coarse meshes obey $h\le1/2$, $1/h=2n\in\mathbb N$, and $1/(2h)=n\in\mathbb N$; [A1] makes every coarse increment the corresponding Brownian increment over its full interval, and [F4] verifies its filtration-relative law and independence. Thus the shared-rate theorem hypotheses hold.

Applying [F1] yields $\operatorname{Var}(\cos(Y_1^h)-\cos(Y_1^{2h}))\le Ch, \qquad |\mathbb E\cos(X_1)-\mathbb E\cos(Y_1^h)|\le C\sqrt h,$ and work $O(h^{-1})$ per coupled path pair. These rates correspond to $(\alpha,\beta)=(1/2,1)$ for this payoff.
